questions.question_text: Explain why it is difficult to track the performance of a direct organic CGM, and suggest one method by which a startup could detect where an organic CGM existed for its product and was operating effectively.
questions.model_answer: It is difficult to track because organic CGMs are word-of-mouth referrals — there is no invitation link or button to click on, so you cannot trace the referral back to its source (1 mark). One detection method: monitor for non-linear (exponential) rises in homepage traffic or app downloads that cannot be attributed to advertising or other linear marketing efforts; this likely indicates word-of-mouth referrals are operating (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for explaining the lack of trackable invitation mechanism. 1 mark for a valid detection method (exponential homepage traffic without corresponding ad spend is the canonical example).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Two-part question — both parts must be answered.

questions.question_text: Explain why a company might operate a content-based indirect CGM using company-generated content at a higher frequency than the product's transaction frequency. Why might the company later decide to attempt to transition the CGM to user-generated content?
questions.model_answer: Operating a content CGM at higher than transaction frequency acts as an awareness/retention mechanism — you cannot make users buy more often, but you can keep reminding them the product exists between buying events (1 mark). Company-generated (CG) content is used initially because the company can decide to produce it, often when the user base is too small to generate enough user content, or when content quality must be controlled (1 mark). Transition to user-generated (UG) content later because UG content is more scalable — you only have so many staff or LLM resources, but a large user base can produce content at scale (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for awareness/reminder rationale; 1 mark for why CG (control / early-stage / cannot get users to write yet); 1 mark for scalability rationale of UG.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Two-part question. Common student error: answering only one part.

questions.question_text: A large, successful consumer internet business with millions of existing users across the world decides to launch a new social media product. To achieve rapid growth, the company implements multiple launch points for the new product within its existing products to convert existing users to also become users of the new product. Within 6 months of launch, the company has acquired tens of millions of users. However, one year later, the active user count is a fraction of this number, and the company closes the product down. With reference to any applicable network effect principles and techniques, give a reasonable explanation as to why this approach was not successful, and suggest a better approach.
questions.model_answer:
**Why the approach failed (1 mark):** Although the company onboarded a large absolute number of users via low-friction sign-up from its existing products, those users had no meaningful relationships with each other on the new product — it was a sparse network. People follow others on the parent product (e.g. Instagram) for different reasons than they would on a new social-media product (e.g. a Twitter-like service), so there was no relevant content from the people they already followed. This created anti-network effects, and external users had no reason to join an empty network. Direct parallel: Google+ pulling Gmail users; Threads pulling Instagram users.

**Better approach (1 mark):** Don't rely on the onboarding trick alone. Help users actively build the right network connections on the new product — ask interest questions during sign-up to suggest relevant follows (Twitter's onboarding pattern), recommend content the user might find interesting on a regular basis (Twitter/TikTok approach), or pay influencers in the relevant space to seed content. More fundamentally, build an atomic network first: prove the product creates value in a small, dense subgroup, then expand outward — recognising this is essentially rebuilding the network from scratch and will take time.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for explaining the sparse-network problem (low friction onboarding ≠ network density on the new product). 1 mark for a credible better approach (interest-based onboarding, recommended content/follows, paid influencers, or atomic-network-first growth). Source: 2024-05-08 revision lecture, Q15.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Question signals 'network effect principles' explicitly — that's your starting point.

questions.question_text: A startup initially operates with one product engineering team that works across all three main areas of its website. During this phase, the product has a consistent design and look-and-feel, but users complain that the features feel unfinished and underpowered. The startup responds by hiring more engineers, so it can split the work into three teams, each dedicated to one of three areas of the product. During this phase, users report the product's depth is stronger, but the product no longer works in a consistent manner across all three areas. Explain which organisational principle or law is applicable here.
questions.model_answer: Conway's Law — organisations ship their organisational structure into the products they build. When the team was unified, the product was consistent but lacked depth. When split into three siloed teams, the team boundaries became product seams, producing inconsistency across areas.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying Conway's Law with brief justification (any words conveying that the product mirrors the org structure).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Only 1 mark — keep answer concise. One sentence sufficient.

questions.question_text: An early-stage startup has a 6-month LTV of $24. Average cost per acquisition (CPA) is $36. Total additional costs to convert these users into revenue-generating users is $1,200 per month. The startup acquires 100 customers per month. Comment on the company's channel acquisition strategy.
questions.model_answer: Step 1 — Compute additional cost per customer: $1,200 / 100 = $12 (1 mark). Step 2 — Compute total CAC: $36 + $12 = $48 (1 mark). Step 3 — Compute LTV:CAC ratio: $24 / $48 = 0.5, i.e. 1:2 (1 mark). Comment: This ratio is well below the 3:1 healthy threshold, and CAC > LTV — the business loses money on every customer acquired. This is unsustainable as a long-term strategy. However, since this is an early-stage startup, it may be deliberate to (a) generate enough users for statistically valid experiments, (b) spike a CGM in its inertial phase, or (c) build atomic/critical-mass networks. Such an approach is acceptable only as a time-limited strategic investment with a clear endpoint (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for working: extracting per-customer additional cost, computing CAC, computing LTV:CAC. Final mark for nuanced commentary acknowledging both unsustainability AND strategic exception. Showing all working secures partial credit even if final number is wrong.
questions.exam_technique_notes: ALWAYS show working. Even if you make an arithmetic error, method marks are awarded. State the conclusion explicitly.

questions.question_text: A cohort retention chart for a typical cohort of a SOCIAL MEDIA PRODUCT shows a steep drop during the first 4 weeks (from 100% down to about 20%), then continues to decline gradually to about 12% by week 24. Comment on the cohort retention performance of this product.
questions.model_answer:
**Explain the shape of the graph (1 mark):** The initial steep drop happens because users are lost during the activation stage, before they have formed a habit around the product. The curve then flattens because users who have formed a habit are less likely to stop using it, so the decay rate reduces. Over the ~6-month (24-week) period, most users are eventually lost.

**Comment on the social-media context (1 mark):** A typical well-performing social media product would be expected to level off around 60–70% active users after the activation period. This product is levelling off at only ~20%, which is very poor for the category — activation is the primary problem and should be the first focus.

**Comment on the long tail (1 mark):** The ongoing retention decline (~20% to ~12% over the next 20 weeks) is not catastrophic — it's slow and steady. Ultimately fatal, but with reasonable time to experiment and improve before it kills the business. So retention work is needed, but secondary to fixing activation.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Mark Logan: 'pay attention to the marks the question's worth' — this is a 3-mark question, so structure your answer in 3 distinct points. Common error: just describing the graph (no marks for that — the question asks why it looks that way). Common error: missing the social-media benchmark (~60–70%). Source: 2025-05-26 revision lecture, Q5.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Pay attention to product type stated in the question — 'social media product' is a clue. Even if uncertain about the benchmark, take a punt: 'I think this is poor for social media' (50/50 to gain a mark, no mark deduction for being wrong).

questions.question_text: How will ChatGPT and similar products affect the dynamics and economics of content-driven indirect compounding growth mechanisms? Explain your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) Lowering the cost of content production (1 mark):** ChatGPT and similar LLMs make it far easier to produce a much greater volume of content with the same number of people — possibly by an order of magnitude. This effectively moves company-generated (CG) content CGMs to behave more like user-generated (UG) ones in terms of scalability. An organisation can therefore get the scale and economic benefits of a UG-content CGM from the start, without having to push through the inertial early phase using a small in-house writing team. Economically, fewer content writers are needed.

**(2) Saturation risk on content channels (1 mark):** If everybody adopts this, the channels where written content is consumed will be flooded. The result is a new kind of saturation — too much material to read, too easy to post — which intensifies competition and may make these channels less effective. The net effect on content-CGM performance may, over time, be neutral once everyone is using LLMs.

**(3) Quality and trust risk (1 mark):** LLM-generated content may be lower quality. Even as quality improves, if users perceive that they are reading machine-generated content they may be put off — there is a loss of the human reader-writer relationship that drives engagement with content CGMs.

**(4) Strategic implication (1 mark):** Content-CGM acquisition performance declines as channels saturate. The value of content shifts toward in-platform retention/awareness (e.g. Medium, LinkedIn keep users engaged when content is being produced) rather than as an acquisition channel. Companies must balance LLM-driven scale against quality control to avoid alienating their audience.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Lecturer: 'identify at least 2 reasons and explain them properly to get full marks; or have more reasons and explain them less deeply'. Look at both pros and cons (dynamics AND economics). Source: 2023-06-06 PM revision lecture, Q14.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Note the word 'Explain' — give reasons, not just descriptions. ChatGPT is a confirmed exam product.

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for TikTok. For each item, state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Network effects:**

**(1) Multi-sided network — viewers ↔ content creators (1 mark):** Viewers are attracted by the volume and quality of short-form videos; creators are attracted by the size of the viewer audience. Each side strengthens the attraction of the other. *(This can alternatively be described as a 3-sided network including advertisers — viewers + creators + advertisers — which scores equivalently.)*

**(2) Multi-sided network — viewers ↔ advertisers (1 mark):** Advertisers are attracted by audience size and the precision of TikTok's targeting; viewers tolerate ads as the price of free content. Strengthens with scale.

**(3) Data-based scale network effect (1 mark):** More usage data → better recommendation algorithm (the For You feed) → more relevant content surfaced → higher engagement → more data. TikTok is particularly known for this effect — short-form videos let it learn user preferences faster than longer-content competitors.

**(4) Brand and purchasing-power scale effects (1 mark):** As TikTok grows, brand recognition makes acquisition easier, and at very large scale TikTok purchases server, storage and bandwidth capacity at increasingly attractive unit prices.

**Compounding growth mechanisms:**

**(5) Indirect content-based CGM — user-generated (1 mark):** Users create short videos which are shared off-platform (Instagram, Twitter/X, WhatsApp, etc.) and bring new users into TikTok.

**(6) Direct invitational CGM (1 mark):** Users directly invite friends to TikTok — driven by social-capital and personal-utility motives (you want your friends on the platform so you can share videos with them).

**(7) Indirect money-based CGM — advertiser side (extra, for safety):** Advertiser revenue funds further investment in product, content moderation, recommendation systems and acquisition advertising — bringing in more users and more advertisers.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per correctly named AND briefly described mechanism, max 6. Lecturer: 'if you described mechanisms but you didn't use the appropriate terminology, you would be more likely to lose marks'. Lecturer warning: 'if you reached out for ChatGPT, you would probably find you had the wrong terminology' — use the course terminology. Source: 2023-06-06 PM revision lecture, Q15 (mechanism inventory verbatim from Mark Logan; one-sentence operational descriptions paraphrased to satisfy the 'brief description of its operation' requirement, since the lecturer named but did not describe each one in the walkthrough).
questions.exam_technique_notes: 6 marks → aim for 6 distinct mechanisms (or 7-8 to be safe). Name properly (e.g. '2-sided network' not just 'network effect') and describe the operation in context of the product.

questions.question_text: Describe the three main types of Acquisition channels.
questions.model_answer: (1) Intent-based channels: users are searching with intent to buy or otherwise complete an action (e.g. SEO, SEM). (2) Awareness-based channels: users do not have intent at the point where ads are presented (e.g. Facebook ads, TV). (3) Referral-based mechanisms: bring new users who have accepted invitations from other users or been indirectly referred to the product (CGMs).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per channel type correctly named and described.
questions.exam_technique_notes: 3 marks = 3 points; 1 per channel.

questions.question_text: Contrast the conversion performance of the three main types of acquisition.
questions.model_answer: Awareness-based channels have the lowest conversion performance (1 mark). Intent and Referral-based mechanisms usually have relatively high conversion performance (1 mark). Referral-based conversion depends on factors such as referrer credibility and the configuration of the referral mechanism (e.g. perceived value of any financial incentive) (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per substantive contrast point.

questions.question_text:
A start-up records the following acquisition performance during a typical month:

(1) Cost of Google SEM Marketing: $80,000
(2) Cost of Facebook Ads: $30,000
(3) Cost of Affiliate Marketing channel: $20,000
(4) Google SEM additional total costs in converting customers to revenue after acquisition: $20,000
(5) Facebook Ads additional total costs: $10,000
(6) Affiliate Marketing additional total costs: $10,000
(7) Google SEM customers acquired: 100
(8) Facebook Ads customers acquired: 100
(9) Affiliate Marketing customers acquired: 100
(10) Google SEM typical retention period: 8 months
(11) Facebook Ads typical retention period: 12 months
(12) Affiliate Marketing typical retention period: 18 months
(13) Typical monthly revenue per customer: $50

State which of these channels has the best performance, justifying your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculate LTV:CAC for each channel. The healthy threshold is 3:1.

**Google SEM (2 marks):**
- CAC = ($80,000 + $20,000) / 100 = $1,000
- LTV = $50 × 8 = $400
- LTV:CAC = 400 / 1,000 = **0.4** — disastrous, loses money on every customer.

**Facebook Ads (1 mark):**
- CAC = ($30,000 + $10,000) / 100 = $400
- LTV = $50 × 12 = $600
- LTV:CAC = 600 / 400 = **1.5** — below the 3:1 threshold, unsustainable long-term.

**Affiliate Marketing (1 mark):**
- CAC = ($20,000 + $10,000) / 100 = $300
- LTV = $50 × 18 = $900
- LTV:CAC = 900 / 300 = **3.0** — meets the healthy 3:1 threshold.

**Conclusion (1 mark):** Affiliate Marketing has the best performance — the only channel meeting the 3:1 LTV:CAC threshold typically required by investors. Google SEM is destroying value (LTV < CAC); Facebook Ads is unsustainable at 1.5:1.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for working out each channel's LTV:CAC + final ranking. Show working — no marks for naked answer. Note: pure arithmetic should be doable in your head or on paper (no calculator).

questions.question_text: You join a start-up as the Growth Director. On your first day, the team boasts to you about an LTV:CAC ratio of 6:1. What questions would you ask, in order to determine the accuracy of this claim?
questions.model_answer: (1) What costs are included between the point of acquisition and the point of revenue generation? (1 mark). (2) Is the CAC segmented by channel and, if so, are we referring to a specific channel or blended-channel CAC? (1 mark). (3) Is the CAC segmented by customer type and, if so, are we referring to a specific customer type or blended-customer CAC? (1 mark). (4) What lifetime value is being used in the calculation, and what assumptions are being made regarding the average revenue per customer and retention period? What data supports those assumptions? (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per substantive diligence question (any 4 of the canonical issues: cost coverage, channel segmentation, customer segmentation, LTV assumptions/retention period).

questions.question_text: Explain why businesses aim to achieve an LTV:CAC ratio of at least 3:1.
questions.model_answer: If CAC > LTV, the acquisition activity loses money on each customer, which is unsustainable (1 mark). LTV being equal to or slightly greater than CAC is insufficient because the business has many other overheads and fixed costs not included in CAC; a ratio of 3:1 or above generally enables profitability after accounting for these costs (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the unsustainability of CAC > LTV; 1 mark for the headroom-for-fixed-costs argument.

questions.question_text: Explain how Growth teams use the Activation Inequality to optimise product activation performance.
questions.model_answer: The Activation Inequality asserts that the value perceived by the user must be greater than the effort perceived to realise that value, otherwise the user will be lost before Stage 1 of Activation is completed (1 mark). Growth and design teams use it when considering, for example, the ordering of steps in the activation process and the amount of information requested from users before delivering value to them (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for stating the inequality; 1 mark for at least one concrete application (step ordering / info-gathering reduction).

questions.question_text: A start-up's activation workflow includes a step that requires the new user to grant access to the user's phone contact list. It then encourages the user to invite friends to use the app before the user can start using the app fully. Comment on the pros and cons of this approach.
questions.model_answer: Pros: likely drives a higher level of referral; users start the referral process before establishing a habit, so even those who do not activate still contribute to referrals. Cons: increases the friction of activation (violates Activation Inequality by adding effort before value), so likely reduces activation rate; delays providing value to the user, also damaging activation. (1 mark for any of these, up to a maximum of 2 marks.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Up to 2 marks for substantive pros AND cons. A balanced answer covering both sides scores higher.

questions.question_text: A cohort retention chart shows seven sequential cohorts of a product, where Cohort 1 is the earliest and Cohort 7 is the latest. The activation performance of the cohorts has been steadily improving from Cohort 1 to Cohort 5. However, in Cohorts 6 and 7, ongoing retention performance shows a new decline. Comment on the cohort trend shown, giving examples of what could be driving this trend.
questions.model_answer: Activation performance for the product is improving over time across the cohort sequence (1 mark). A likely explanation is that the start-up is experimenting with activation workflow improvements (1 mark). In Cohorts 6 and 7, there is a new decline in ongoing retention performance (1 mark). This could have been caused by an experiment or feature introduction that has damaged retention — e.g. a recently shipped change to the core experience or a degraded onboarding step (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for: identifying improving activation, plausible explanation, identifying late-cohort retention regression, plausible cause for regression.

questions.question_text: Explain the composition (i.e. the structure) of a retention metric. How do Growth teams decide which specific retention metric to use?
questions.model_answer: Structure: NaP, where N = number of times an action is performed, a = the name of the action, P = the period in which it is performed. The metric quantifies the intensity and frequency of an action that correlates most strongly with future user retention (2 marks for the structural points). Setting the metric: examine how actions at given frequencies and intensities correlate with future retention; the stronger the correlation, the better the candidate metric (1 mark). In early stages where there is insufficient traffic or time, choose a reasonable candidate and refine over time (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks for structure (NaP definition); 1 mark for correlation-based selection; 1 mark for early-stage refinement strategy.

questions.question_text: A Retention-Cohort Table for a product shows the number of customers still active in each of the weeks following sign-up, across multiple cohorts. By examining the data, comment on the cohort trend and provide a reasonable interpretation. What action should the team take? (Note: this question type is unlikely in the current exam since data download is no longer permitted, but the question is still useful for revision.)
questions.model_answer: Transpose the absolute counts into a cohort percentage decay table (normalised to either previous month or base month) — this exposes patterns hidden in absolute numbers (1 mark). The decay table will show whether activation has worsened (e.g. one cohort with notably worse early retention) or whether ongoing retention has changed. If Cohort 7 (or the most recent) shows worse activation, this is most likely due to a recent change in the product's activation flow or marketing activities (1 mark). The team should: review all experiments, feature changes, and marketing activity changes introduced at that time, and determine whether a change needs rolling back; also check seasonal and external market factors (2 marks).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for normalisation strategy; 1 mark for diagnosing activation regression; 2 marks for action plan (experiment review + rollback + external factor check).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Per Mark Logan: this question form is no longer used in exams since data downloads are not permitted. Useful for revision only.

questions.question_text: Comment on the suitability of the following retention metric for a Tax Return Calculation package: 4r28, where r = review tax details.
questions.model_answer: This is an inappropriate metric for most months of the year because tax products tend to be used yearly — both the period (28 days) and the number of uses (4) are too frequent in general (1 mark). However, during the tax-return season itself, this metric may be more appropriate as users genuinely review their details multiple times across a few weeks (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying the mismatch with annual usage; 1 mark for the seasonal nuance.

questions.question_text: Explain why Growth teams sometimes use two different content-based Indirect CGM subtypes in sequence, as part of a growth strategy.
questions.model_answer: There are two main sub-types of Content-based indirect CGM: Company-Generated content (CG) and User-Generated content (UG) (1 mark). CG is easier to move through the inertial phase but harder to scale; UG has the opposite characteristics. Combining them in sequence — start with CG, then add UG — captures the advantages of both (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying both sub-types; 1 mark for the start-CG-then-UG rationale.

questions.question_text: Explain how a start-up should decide which sub-type of Direct Compounding Growth Mechanism is likely to be most effective for its product.
questions.model_answer: Three sub-types exist: Personal Utility-based, Financial, and Social Capital-based (1 mark). A start-up where users experience significant benefit from the referral itself (in terms of subsequent product value, e.g. messaging apps) prefers a Personal Utility model (1 mark). The Financial sub-type is better when no such 'selfish benefit' exists. Social Capital effects often supplement the first two but can drive referral when no direct benefit exists and the business model cannot sustain a financial mechanism (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Up to 3 marks for explaining the three sub-types and the criteria for choosing among them.

questions.question_text: Explain the relationship between Business-Model <-> Channel Fit and Financial Asymmetry in financially-incentivised Compounding Growth Mechanisms.
questions.model_answer: Business-Model <-> Channel Fit requires that the cost of acquiring customers through a channel is sustainably supportable by the revenue earned from those customers. If a CGM's financial incentive is too large relative to LTV, this requirement is not met and the mechanism will ultimately lose the business money. Financial Asymmetry — where the perceived value of the incentive to the user can exceed the actual cost to the business (e.g. a free month of a subscription product) — helps make financial CGMs viable while preserving Business-Model <-> Channel Fit.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for explaining the constraint (BM-channel fit) AND the lever (asymmetry) that allows financial incentives to remain affordable.

questions.question_text: Explain what is meant by the Starvation Phase of a Compounding Growth Loop. What action should the start-up take during this phase: continue as before, increase time optimising this mechanism, or reduce focus on the mechanism? Why?
questions.model_answer: In the starvation phase, the number of potential new users reachable by the mechanism begins to saturate (1 mark). Maintaining the same strategy as in the growth phase yields diminishing results, as would increasing focus (1 mark). Better to redirect resources to either establishing a new mechanism, changing the market in which the mechanism operates, or another significant contextual change — i.e. reduce focus on this mechanism (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the saturation explanation; 1 mark for the diminishing-returns logic; 1 mark for the redirect action and rationale.

questions.question_text: Explain the operation of an n-sided network. Give an example of a well-known product based on an n-sided network as part of your answer.
questions.model_answer: In general network effects, the greater the participation in the network, the greater the value to its participants — which attracts further participants in a self-reinforcing loop (1 mark). In an n-sided network, there are n types of participant; one type acts as an attractor for other types (1 mark). Example: Facebook consists of users, advertisers, and content providers. The presence of users attracts content providers; content from those providers attracts additional users; both attract advertisers (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the basic network-effects concept; 1 mark for the n-sided structure; 1 mark for a valid example with explanation.

questions.question_text: Explain how start-ups attempt to manage liquidity in the earliest stages of a 2-sided network's lifetime.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity in a 2-sided network concerns ensuring sufficient and balanced supply and demand. In an early-stage network, there is usually a lack of both (1 mark for explaining the basic problem). Supply-side techniques: incentivise suppliers to join, compensate them for lack of earnings, actively recruit (1 mark for two examples). Demand-side techniques: drive referral mechanisms with incentives, unsustainable advertising, discounting (1 mark for two examples).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the liquidity problem; 1 mark for two supply-side techniques; 1 mark for two demand-side techniques.

questions.question_text: Explain how, in a 2-sided network, network effects can strengthen the growth performance of compounding growth mechanisms at the demand-side of the network.
questions.model_answer: The 2-sided network attracts more users to the demand-side because they are drawn by the available supply on the other side (1 mark). This means the demand-side CGM is acting upon a greater number of users in each iteration, generating more returns per cycle (1 mark). Network attraction also creates more impetus for referred users to join the product, since the perceived value of joining is higher when supply is plentiful (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for: (1) network attraction increases demand-side population; (2) more users in each CGM iteration → more output; (3) higher join intent for referees due to value of network.

questions.question_text: Explain why compounding growth mechanisms rarely work well on the supply-side of a 2-sided network, in contrast to the demand-side, where they are often very effective.
questions.model_answer: At the supply-side, participants are often in competition with each other; there is little or no incentive operating that would drive referral behaviour.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the competition-disincentive explanation.

questions.question_text: Explain, with reference to any applicable principles, why it is very difficult for an organization that is highly focussed on its internal functional hierarchy to successfully optimize the Growth Model's Customer Journey.
questions.model_answer: The Customer Journey requires multiple skillsets to work closely together AND requires the organisation to focus on this process continuously. This is harder if the organisation is structured around skill-based silos and does not routinely combine people from different skill-areas into teams (2 marks). Conway's Law: organisations tend to mirror their organisational structures in the products they build (1 mark). In this case, Conway's Law predicts that a purely functional hierarchy will create interfaces between teams that disrupt the requirement to work as a single integrated team on the Customer Journey (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks for the multi-skill / sustained-focus argument; 1 mark for stating Conway's Law; 1 mark for applying it to this scenario.

questions.question_text: In the context of the Lean Start-up methodology, what properties distinguish Learning Metrics from Vanity Metrics?
questions.model_answer: Learning Metrics: express a measure of activity; therefore frequency-based. Vanity Metrics: typically simple accumulators with no relationship to frequency.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for the activity/frequency vs accumulator distinction.

questions.question_text: A founding team of a small start-up iterates rapidly by quickly making all of the decisions in the business. This is very effective. However, when the team grows to 40 people in size, the CEO realises that, despite working the same way as before, the speed of iteration of the business has considerably reduced. Explain what is most probably causing this velocity reduction.
questions.model_answer: The business is slowing because decisions are being overly centralised at a scale where this model no longer fits (1 mark). Decision latency has increased, and decision intensity drops proportional to the SQUARE of decision latency, significantly reducing iteration speed (1 mark). This also affects employee morale and sense of agency, further reducing iteration speed; eventually the founders become overloaded, worsening the problem (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for centralisation; 1 mark for decision latency / decision intensity; 1 mark for compounding effects (morale, overload).

questions.question_text: With reference to the previous question, what general approach should the founders consider to improve the performance of the business on a sustainable basis going forward?
questions.model_answer: Push agency to the front-line of the business, as an organisational strategic goal. (Half mark for 'they should make less decisions themselves' or similar without naming the agency principle.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming agency-pushing as the strategic answer; half-mark for the weaker formulation.

questions.question_text: Explain the differences between the investment stages Seed, Series A and Series B.
questions.model_answer: These stages relate to different growth points in a start-up. Seed capital is typically less than $2 million, corresponding to the stage where the start-up is seeking product-market fit. Series A is typically awarded to drive growth and is of the order of $10 million. Series B ($30m+) and later stages are typically larger, to further drive growth.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Marks for distinguishing each stage by typical size and company stage.

questions.question_text: The concept of growth models doesn't just apply to modern tech start-ups and scale-ups. Disney Corporation has been described historically using a growth-flywheel diagram (Walt Disney, 1957). More recently, Disney launched the Disney+ streaming service. Using your knowledge of this service and any available material you can find on the internet, describe the growth model for Disney+.
questions.model_answer: Up to 5 marks for any 5 of: (1) Aggregator Effect: Disney+ is the only streaming service where all Disney assets can be viewed, attracting Disney fans; the more content Disney creates, the stronger this effect. (2) Money-based CGM: subscription revenue → buy ads → sign-ups → subscription revenue, often spiked with extra paid-marketing spend to seed other CGMs. (3) Organic direct CGM: subscription revenue → fund new content → users watch and tell friends by word-of-mouth → some sign up. (4) Content-based indirect CGM: account sharing with up to 7 users (4 simultaneous devices) eventually creates pressure for some users to sign up for their own account. (5) Activation/Activation Inequality: free trial period demonstrates value before requiring payment. (6) Engagement Intensity: regular new content (movies, box sets), Group Watch feature, in-app recommendation engine, auto-start next episode, regular emails, multiple user profiles.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for each of any 5 distinct mechanisms (or similar). Listing 6+ provides safety margin.
questions.exam_technique_notes: 5 marks → aim for 5+ mechanisms. Always name the mechanism type AND describe its operation in the product's context.

questions.question_text: Swipii is an app-based start-up that enables shoppers to receive cash-back when they make purchases in shops. New users first link their debit cards then sign up. Whenever they shop in a Swipii-affiliated store, they receive cashback into their Swipii account. Businesses can offer special offers (e.g. 10% cashback on a coffee purchased before 10:00am on a Tuesday). Swipii is therefore a two-sided network of shoppers and shops. When Swipii enters a new country, which is the better strategy: target some shops across as many cities as possible, or focus on just one or two cities at a time? Explain your answer.
questions.model_answer: Swipii should concentrate on one or two cities at a time. (1) Referral mechanisms work better with critical mass, which is more achievable when efforts are concentrated in one city (1 mark). (2) As a 2-sided network, it is easier to create an Atomic Network in a small area first; once it is proven, expansion is easier (1 mark). Credit also given for: focusing on one city makes it easier to learn and test user experience quickly to establish PMF in the new market.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for the referral/critical-mass argument; 1 mark for the atomic-network argument. Alternative: PMF/learning-speed argument also creditable.

questions.question_text: An early-stage start-up acquires 1,000 customers a month on average, at an average CPA of $80. The start-up uses a sales team to convert customer leads to revenue-generating customers, at a total salary cost of $120,000 per year. The start-up estimates its 6-month customer LTV to be $300. Comment on the company's channel acquisition strategy.
questions.model_answer:
**Step 1 — sales cost per customer (1 mark):** Annual salary $120,000 ÷ annual customer volume (12 × 1,000 = 12,000) = **$10 per customer**.

**Step 2 — total CAC (1 mark):** Channel CPA $80 + sales cost $10 = **$90 per customer**.

**Step 3 — LTV:CAC ratio (1 mark):** $300 / $90 = **3.33**.

**Step 4 — conclusion (1 mark):** The ratio exceeds the 3:1 threshold investors typically require, meaning acquisition is profitable with headroom to cover other fixed costs. The acquisition strategy is sound.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks for the calculation chain (sales-cost-per-customer, total CAC, ratio); 1 mark for the soundness conclusion with reference to the 3:1 threshold. Watch the units: salary is annual, customers are monthly — must annualise the customer count before dividing.

questions.question_text: Explain why Intent-based channels usually exhibit a higher conversion rate than Awareness-based channels. Why are Awareness-based channels still used despite this difference in conversion rates?

Awareness-based channels are still used because they build brand awareness and reduce the likelihood that users forget about the business — they also typically improve performance of intent-based channels by making the brand recognisable when users do search (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for each part.

questions.question_text: In what circumstances is it appropriate to operate with CAC > LTV?

questions.question_text: Explain what is meant by the Inertial Phase of a Compounding Growth mechanism. Provide one example from each of two separate businesses (i.e. two examples in total) of approaches to overcome this inertia.

questions.question_text: A cohort retention chart shows the performance of seven sequential newly acquired user cohorts. Cohorts 1-3 improve steadily. Cohort 4 performs relatively badly during activation and then recovers somewhat. Cohorts 5-7 resume the improvement trend, with some Cohort 4 users moving out of dormancy in later periods. Comment on the sequence and provide an explanation for any anomalies.

questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for general improvement; 1 mark for identifying the Cohort 4 anomaly; 2 marks for a plausible mechanism that explains BOTH the activation dip AND the eventual recovery / later cohort restoration.

questions.question_text: A founder-CEO of a rapidly growing technology start-up laments to her co-founders that engineers don't release features as quickly as was the case when she and her co-founders were doing all the work, and that everything just seems to take longer now. questions.question_text: What are the three typical patterns shown on a retention-cohort graph? For each, state what it indicates about the business.
questions.model_answer: (1) Green line — drops then levels off; users have formed habits and retention has stabilised; if most cohorts look like this, the business has PMF. (2) Yellow line — continues falling slowly; retention is not catastrophic but needs improvement; common in early-stage start-ups. (3) Red line — falls rapidly toward zero; the business is heading for failure unless retention is significantly improved.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per pattern correctly described and interpreted.

questions.question_text: Explain the structure of a retention metric (NaP). Give two rules for setting a good NaP metric and explain why each rule matters.
questions.model_answer: Structure: NaP — N = number of times an action is performed, a = the specific action, P = the time period in days (1 mark for structure). Rule 1: N should be greater than 1, because this gives a better signal-to-noise ratio and reduces false churn signals — if N=1, a single missed action would falsely flag a user as churning (1.5 marks). Rule 2: P should be greater than the typical usage cycle of the product. For example, if the product is used mainly on weekdays, P=1 day would create false churn signals on weekends (1.5 marks).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for structure; up to 1.5 marks per rule with explanation of why it matters.

questions.question_text: A tax return software company uses the retention metric 4r28 (4 tax reviews every 28 days). Comment on the suitability of this metric.

questions.question_text: Explain the Activation Inequality. How do growth teams use it to optimise onboarding?

Growth teams use it to optimise the ordering of steps in activation and to minimise the amount of information requested before delivering value — value demonstration should come before heavy info gathering (1 mark).

questions.question_text: A CGM has V = 0.5. Calculate the Growth Multiplier. If an experiment improves V to 0.6, what is the new Growth Multiplier? Comment on the significance of this improvement.
questions.model_answer:
**Original Growth Multiplier (1 mark):** GM = 1 / (1 − V) = 1 / (1 − 0.5) = 1 / 0.5 = **2.0**.

**New Growth Multiplier after experiment (1 mark):** GM = 1 / (1 − 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = **2.5**.

**Significance (1 mark):** A change in V of just 10 percentage points (0.5 → 0.6) produces a 25% uplift in GM (2.0 → 2.5). This demonstrates the **compounding amplification** of CGMs: small improvements in cycle-to-cycle conversion parameters amplify through the loop into disproportionately large gains in total users acquired before exhaustion.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per GM calculation; 1 mark for the compounding-significance commentary. Numbers chosen to be no-calculator friendly: 1/0.5 = 2 and 1/0.4 = 2.5 are mental arithmetic.

(2)   Cost of Facebook Ads:  $51121
(3)   Cost of financial incentives in compounding growth mechanism:   $15341
(4)   Additional average cost per customer in converting customers to revenue after acquisition:  $37.9
(5)   Number of customers acquired: 1451

Calculate the minimum Customer LTV required to make January's acquisition costs self-funding. In your answer, ignore any other business overheads not listed above. Round your final answer to zero decimal places. Do NOT include a $ dollar sign in your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Recognise the question type:** This is a self-funding question (LTV = CAC), NOT a 3:1 LTV/CAC investor question. To be self-funding, LTV needs to at least equal CAC.

**Step 1 — Add monthly channel and CGM costs:** Google SEM ($123,801) + Facebook Ads ($51,121) + financial incentives in CGM ($15,341) = **$190,263**.

**Step 2 — Convert per-customer conversion cost to monthly total:** $37.9 is per customer, so multiply by customers acquired: 1,451 × $37.9 ≈ **$54,993**.

**Step 3 — Total acquisition cost for January:** $190,263 + $54,993 ≈ **$245,256**.

**Step 4 — Per-customer cost (= CAC):** $245,256 / 1,451 ≈ **$169** per customer.

**Step 5 — Minimum LTV for self-funding:** LTV must equal CAC, so minimum LTV ≈ **169**.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Each student got slightly different parameter values, so don't worry if answers differ. Leeway built in — small rounding errors still earn the marks. Recognise this is a self-funding (LTV = CAC) question, not a 3:1 LTV/CAC investor question. Don't forget to convert the per-customer conversion cost into a monthly total before adding it in. Note: 2023 format used calculators; calculate manually using simple arithmetic for 2026 exam.

questions.question_text:
A product has a Direct, Financially-Incentivised CGM with a growth multiplier of 2.98.

Calculate the cycle-to-cycle sign-up ratio for this mechanism. Give your answer to two decimal places.
questions.model_answer:
**Recall the formula:** GM = 1 / (1 − V), where V is the cycle-to-cycle sign-up ratio (viral coefficient). This question gives GM and asks for V — rearrange the formula.

**Step 1 — Rearrange:** V = 1 − 1/GM.

**Step 2 — Plug in GM = 2.98:** V = 1 − 1/2.98 = 1 − 0.3356 ≈ **0.66**.

Final answer: **0.66** (to two decimal places).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Each student's paper had different parameter values. Just rearrange the formula correctly — straightforward arithmetic. Mark says: 'pretty simple mathematics for finalist students as long as we don't panic about the question.'

questions.question_text:
The chart shows two lines on a logarithmic time axis (0 to 5 years): a CPA line (red) and an LTV/CAC line.

With reference to concepts from the course, interpret the CPA profile (red line) over time, identifying and explaining the three main phases.
questions.model_answer:
**Three phases — one mark each — explain WHY each phase has its shape, not just describe it:**

**Phase 1 (low and falling):** CPA starts relatively low and falls lower. The channel is new with limited competition, and the organisation is learning and optimising on it, driving cost-per-acquisition down.

**Phase 2 (stable plateau):** CPA reaches a relatively stable, low level for a period. The organisation has done all the optimisation it reasonably can; competition hasn't yet ramped up, so CPA plateaus.

**Phase 3 (rising sharply):** CPA begins to rise — gradually at first as competition arrives in the channel, then aggressively/exponentially as the channel saturates. More companies pile in, channel suppliers can charge more, and it becomes a runaway effect.

(Reversing stages 2 and 3 in your description — plateau followed by steep rise — also earns full marks.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Common errors: (1) talking about CPA versus LTV/CAC — the question is about CPA only; (2) saying 'CPA starts higher than LTV/CAC then falls' — these are on different axes with different units (one is a ratio, one is a cost), so they CANNOT be compared quantitatively, only qualitatively in terms of how they're moving; (3) just describing the shape without explaining causes scores nothing. You MUST cover all three phases — focusing too much on one or two phases loses marks.

questions.question_text: Using the same graph as Q11, interpret the LTV/CAC line over time, identifying and explaining the three main phases with reference to course concepts.
questions.model_answer:
**Setup:** LTV/CAC is a ratio — ask what's changing and why it would move. Numerator = LTV; denominator = CAC (of which CPA is one component).

**Stage 1 (rising rapidly):** LTV/CAC rises rapidly, mirroring the INVERSE of CPA — because CPA is falling rapidly, the denominator gets smaller, so the ratio gets bigger.

**Stage 2 (rising more slowly):** CPA is now relatively stable, but LTV/CAC continues to improve. This must be due to either (a) LTV increasing (numerator getting bigger) or (b) other components of CAC beyond channel cost getting smaller (e.g. better conversion of channel arrivals into customers), or both — credit either point.

**Stage 3 (falling rapidly):** LTV/CAC falls rapidly. Even though LTV may still be improving and other CAC components may still be improving, the rise in CPA at this stage is so large that it dominates, making CAC bigger and bigger and ultimately bringing LTV/CAC down.

**Summary:** CPA dominates at the start and end; in the middle, LTV improvements or other CAC improvements explain the continued rise.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Slightly harder than Q11 but you've been warmed up by it. The key insight is that you must EXPLAIN the middle phase by reference to LTV growth or non-channel CAC reductions, since CPA alone doesn't account for it. Same axis-comparison warning as Q11 applies.

questions.question_text:
*⚠ Reconstructed from explainer-VTT framing.*

With reference to concepts studied in the course, explain possible ways in which Musk's decision (on returning as CEO of Twitter) to unban previously-banned users such as Donald Trump may affect Twitter's number of active users over time.
questions.model_answer:
**Three marks = at least three good points (more won't earn more — be concise). MUST cover BOTH positive and negative effects for full marks.**

**Negative / anti-network-effect points:**

**(1) User exodus:** Users may depart the platform because there's too much negative or inappropriate content, or because they're offended by the reputations of those who've returned — anti-network effect on users.

**(2) Advertiser exodus:** The same point applies to advertisers leaving (Twitter's ad revenues fell dramatically since Musk's return — partly due to unbannings, partly to general chaos and layoff handling).

**(3) Brand damage:** Anti-network effect on the brand.

**Positive points (must consider these too):**

**(4) Shareability of controversial content:** More controversial content is more shareable and more attractive to new users — we see this on Facebook where algorithms deliberately promote controversial content.

**(5) High-follower-count return:** The unbanned users had very high follower counts and may have lost interest while away — bringing them back brings their audiences back / increases shareability.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: You MUST consider both the positive and negative effects to get full marks. Discussing only anti-network effects caps you below full marks. Reference course terminology (anti-network effects, shareability, network value).

questions.question_text:
*⚠ Reconstructed from explainer-VTT framing. Mark count estimated (Mark didn't state it explicitly).*

Explain how ChatGPT and similar products affect the dynamics and economics of content-driven indirect compounding growth mechanisms. Explain your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Setup:** Two types of content-driven indirect CGM — user-generated (UGC) and company-generated (CG). The traditional bottleneck: CG content scales with employed writers, so it has a low ceiling; UGC scales with users.

**Point 1 — Lowering CG content cost / raising scale:** ChatGPT and similar tools let a company produce far more content (potentially an order of magnitude more) with the same number of people. Effectively moves CG-content CGMs to behave like UGC-content CGMs in scaling — the company gets the scale and economics of UGC right from the start, without bootstrapping a small in-house writing team past the early stage.

**Point 2 — Channel saturation risk:** If everybody adopts this, channels get flooded with content — a new type of saturation. Channels where written content is consumed may become less effective. Net effectiveness over time may be neutral once everyone is using LLMs.

**Point 3 — Quality and trust risk:** LLM-generated content may be lower quality. Even as quality improves, if users perceive content is machine-generated they may be put off — there's a loss of human reader-writer relationship.

**Point 4 — Strategic implication:** Content-CGM acquisition performance declines as channels saturate. Value of content shifts toward in-platform retention/awareness (Medium, LinkedIn) rather than acquisition. Companies must balance LLM-driven scale against quality control.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Identify at least 2 reasons and explain them properly, OR more reasons explained less deeply — both can earn full marks. Look at pros and cons. Some students answered about ChatGPT's marketing performance — the question is nothing to do with that and gets no marks.

questions.question_text:
*⚠ Reconstructed from explainer-VTT framing. Mark count estimated (Mark didn't state it explicitly).*

List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for TikTok. For each item, state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Each correctly named mechanism scores a mark, provided it's properly named with course terminology.**

**Network effects:**

**(1) One-sided network of users attracting users.**

**(2) Multi-sided network of users, content providers and advertisers.** Can frame as two two-sided networks (users + advertisers; users/readers + content creators) — but framing as a single three-sided network shows more depth and earns more.

**(3) Brand-scale network effect.** Recognition makes acquisition easier.

**(4) Data-scale network effect.** TikTok is famous for these — its recommendation engine improves with more usage data.

**(5) Purchasing-power scale effect.** TikTok can buy server/storage capacity at increasingly attractive prices at scale.

**CGMs:**

**(6) Indirect money-based CGM (advertisers).** Advertiser revenue funds more product investment.

**(7) Indirect content-based CGM.** UGC shared off-platform brings new users back to TikTok.

**(8) Direct invitational CGM (users inviting users).** Sub-divide by motive into:
- **(9) Social-capital-based CGMs.**
- **(10) Personal-utility CGMs** — you want your friends on the platform to share videos with.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: If you described mechanisms but didn't use the appropriate terminology you'd lose marks. Reaching for ChatGPT here gave you the wrong terminology AND attracted further markdown for using ChatGPT, so you scored less. Most people scored well on this question PROVIDED they had time to finish it.

questions.question_text:
A product tracks performance using monthly active users (MAU) and monthly revenue. The MAU graph is stable for many months then suddenly falls, while the revenue graph declines roughly linearly over the same period.

(a) Give an explanation for the performance experienced during this period, accounting for the difference between the revenue profile and the active-user profile.

(b) Suggest a change to the metrics being used by the company that would improve its ability to track product market performance.
questions.model_answer:
**Part (a) — Explanation (~2 marks):** This is a classic case of an active-user/retention metric using the WRONG measurement period. Users are reducing their engagement intensity over time — that's what's causing the steady decline in revenue. But this drop in intensity doesn't show up in the MAU count because of how the metric is defined: if you use a product 10 times a month and I use it once a month, MAU counts us both as active. The metric won't distinguish us, even though you're generating much more revenue (more purchases, more ad views). So as users drop their engagement intensity, MAU stays flat — until engagement falls below once-a-month and users stop showing up at all, at which point MAU falls suddenly off a cliff. The revenue graph reflected the true underlying decline all along.

**Part (b) — Metric change (~1 mark):** Change the frequency of the active-users metric to weekly or daily — that would have tracked the revenue graph much more closely and surfaced the problem far earlier.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Roughly 2 marks for the explanation, 1 for the metric-change suggestion. Partial credit awarded for answers like 'users moved from a paid tier to an unpaid tier and then stopped using the product' — not as clean an explanation, but in the right ballpark.

questions.question_text:
*⚠ Reconstructed from explainer-VTT framing. Mark count estimated.*

With reference to concepts covered in the course, explain the effect that Twitter's feature — requiring users to open an article before sharing it with other users — may have on its user network size. Discuss at least two aspects, with relevant course concepts accurately stated, for full marks.
questions.model_answer:
**Approach:** Pros-and-cons answer. Don't have to be 'right' about what actually happened — put correct course concepts into play.

**Positive (pro) side:**

**(1) Retention benefit — content quality:** If users must engage with content before sharing, the content circulating on average is higher quality (because users have actually checked it out and decided to share). Higher-quality circulating content has a positive retention effect — users stay engaged with the platform.

**(2) Acquisition benefit — quality halo:** When users share that higher-quality content externally, new users are attracted to a network associated with quality content. Reference: brand/trust, network effects on retention, retention-loop mechanisms, content-based CGMs.

**Negative (con) side:**

**(3) Friction effect:** Users perceive more friction before sharing, so they're less likely to bother sharing — slows network growth.

**(4) Retention loops weaker:** Less sharing → retention loops become less effective.

**(5) Engagement intensity drop:** Added friction may make users decide the platform is no longer as valuable, so they engage less; reduced engagement intensity may eventually lead to a reduction in active users.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for description, 1 for explanation, 1 for properly referencing the terminology behind these concepts. Discuss two aspects (e.g. one positive, one negative) for full marks. Use course terminology accurately.

questions.question_text:
*⚠ Reconstructed from explainer-VTT framing. Mark count estimated.*

A CRM software vendor focuses on large-scale enterprise customers and uses a sales team combined with extensive advertising at conferences. After several years, in response to slowing global sales, the CEO decides to launch a new freemium version of the product aimed at smaller businesses. With reference to concepts studied in the course, comment on this decision and explain what factors the company should consider when developing a growth plan.
questions.model_answer:
**Frame using lecture 1 strategy and the Four-Fits model:**

**Recognise the strategic move (~1 mark):** The basic startup strategy is find product-market fit, then grow that market as far as you can, then — as growth tops out — move into a new adjacency (new product category, new geography, new customer category) and find product-market fit there. The company is approaching saturation in its current market and is sensibly moving into a new adjacency.

**Then structure the rest using the Four-Fits model:**

**(1) Product-Market Fit (~1 mark):** Will the existing product be relevant to smaller businesses? May need feature changes / simplification.

**(2) Business Model–Market Fit (~1 mark):** Freemium changes how much revenue is earned per customer. Are there enough smaller businesses willing to pay enough to meet the company's revenue goals?

**(3) Business Model–Channel Fit (~1 mark):** Freemium implies selling online without sales people. Can the company afford to keep using sales people to convert smaller, lower-revenue customers? The channel mix needs to change.

**(4) Product-Channel Fit (~1 mark):** Previous channels (sales team, conference advertising) may not be appropriate for the smaller-business customer set — the channel mix needs revisiting (likely more self-service, content marketing, etc.).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Some students wrote at length about freemium models (pricing tiers, conversion between tiers etc.) — that's literally correct but the course doesn't focus on it; it'll get some credit but far less than answers using the Four-Fits model and market-adjacency concepts. The phrase 'with reference to concepts studied in the course' is a clue. ChatGPT-generated answers tend to focus on freemium mechanics and score lower for the same reason.

questions.model_answer:
**Largest question on the paper — apply everything we've covered to the metaverse domain.**

**(a) Acquisition strategy & channel approach:** Use the Four-Fits model to plan a balanced channel mix (linear channels + CGMs) for reaching metaverse-style customers. Discuss dynamics — e.g. running channels at a loss initially to bootstrap the network, then transitioning to CGM-based channels later.

**(b) Activation & retention (4 marks):** Activation — invoke the activation model and the activation inequality; arrange the on-boarding process accordingly (let users quickly create a generic avatar/habitat and try out most features before being asked for more information). Retention — features that increase engagement intensity and bring users back; engagement frequency, real frequency. Crucial: contextualise to the actual product — don't just regurgitate slides.

**(c) Monetization (up to 2 marks):** Virtual currency in the game; subscription model; in-game purchases; advertisers paying for real estate inside the virtual world. Each valid item earns a mark up to 2.

**(d) CGMs / network effects / bootstrapping / anti-network effects:**
- Network effects: building a one-sided users-attract-users network first, then growing to add advertisers and content creators (multi-sided); reaching scale where scale-based effects (brand, data, purchasing-power) kick in.
- CGMs: direct invitational CGM (inviting users to interact with you inside the virtual world — personal-utility plus social-capital), and a financially-incentivised CGM rewarding virtual game currency (ties into monetization).
- Bootstrapping: focus on the hard side of the network. You must identify who the hard side is (could be a subset of users, could be content creators) — there isn't a single 'right' answer; demonstrate intelligent thinking. Atomic-network approach also valid — growing constituencies in one interest group, then expanding.
- Anti-network effects: squarely social-media territory — trolling, fake news, online bullying — describe in course terms.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Per-section marks given in question. Answers must be contextualised to the actual metaverse domain — don't just recite generic concept notes. If you describe mechanisms but don't name the concept, you get half marks per answer. ChatGPT scores lower because it doesn't use course terminology. Many students were short on time at this point — short note-form answers still earned some marks. Mark advised students before the exam to do background research on metaverse-style products; later students should do the same before attempting.

questions.question_text:
A start-up records the following channel costs in a typical month:

(1)   Cost of Google SEM:  €40000

(2)   Cost of Facebook Ads:  €30000

The start-up also incurs additional costs each month to fully convert potential leads arriving on the above channels. It acquires, on average, 100 paying customers per month.

The start-up achieves an average customer Lifetime Value of €3000.

If the LTV:CAC ratio must satisfy the expectations of potential investors, calculate how much the start-up can afford to spend in total each month on converting channel leads into paying customers.

In your answer, ignore any other business overheads not listed above. Round your final answer to zero decimal places. Do NOT include a € sign in your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Step 1 — Identify the required LTV:CAC ratio:** The question says the ratio must satisfy the expectations of potential investors, so we know it has to be at least **3:1**.

**Step 2 — Work backwards from LTV to allowable CAC:** With LTV of €3000 and a 3:1 ratio, the allowable CAC per customer is €3000 / 3 = **€1000 per customer**.

**Step 3 — Calculate total allowable monthly spend:** Because there are 100 customers a month, total allowable monthly spend = 100 × €1000 = **€100,000**.

**Step 4 — Subtract the channel costs already being spent:** Already spending €40,000 + €30,000 = €70,000 on channels. Headroom for conversion costs = €100,000 − €70,000 = **€30,000**.

Final answer: **30000**.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks total. Partial credit: if you calculate the per-customer CAC but forget to multiply by 100 customers, you would still get 1 of 2. Workflow Mark emphasises: (1) use LTV to derive total allowable CAC, (2) subtract the costs already given to find the headroom for conversion costs, (3) remember to multiply up to a monthly total.

questions.question_text:
BeReal is a social media app whose main feature is that users utilise the app to simultaneously take one photo of themselves and their environment at the same time of day every day, which are then uploaded to the BeReal social network. To encourage them to do so, users can only see the images posted by other users on that day if they first perform the above action.

Using specific concepts and techniques studied on this course, comment on the effectiveness of this approach from a retention perspective.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Habit formation positive (1 mark):** Doing something daily encourages habit formation, which is good for engagement and retention.

**Point 2 — Low intensity for a social-media product (1 mark):** Single use per day is not particularly high intensity for a social-media app — although habit formation appears strong, the actual engagement intensity is relatively low for the social-media category, so it isn't a perfect model. (Credit also given for noting that users do spend additional time looking at other people's photos, which boosts intensity somewhat.)

**Point 3 — Fixed time-of-day problem (1 mark, alternative to point 2 or 4):** A fixed time of day might not suit every user — they may not always be able to make the suggested time. So although habit formation seems healthy in principle (doing something every day), in practice the user might not be able to do it daily — an engagement-intensity issue.

**Point 4 — Forced low-quality content (1 mark, alternative):** Daily forced postings create more content (good for content CGMs), but the content may be poor in quality because users sometimes do it reluctantly, which can hurt the experience for viewers.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks. Mark says the question was 'marked quite freely' on ideas revolving around these principles. The key thing he is looking for is awareness that this is fundamentally an engagement-intensity question and that there are pluses and minuses to the model. 1 mark for the habit-formation point, plus 1 mark for any 2 of the 3 follow-on points (low intensity / fixed time / forced low-quality content).

questions.question_text:
A start-up deploys a Personal Utility-based, Direct CGM with a growth multiplier of 2.0.

In a test, 2000 users obtained from linear marketing are used to seed the CGM, which runs through multiple cycles until exhaustion.

Calculate how many additional users are obtained from completion of the first cycle of the CGM, i.e. with how many users does the second cycle commence? Assume there exists no noise or error rate in the data.

Give your answer to zero decimal places.
questions.model_answer:
**Step 1 — Recall the growth-multiplier formula:** GM = 1 / (1 − v), where GM is the growth multiplier and v is the per-cycle viral coefficient (cycle-to-cycle sign-up ratio). We are given GM = 2.0 but not v — so the question requires us to rearrange.

**Step 2 — Solve for v:** Rearranging gives v = 1 − 1/GM = 1 − 1/2 = **0.5**.

**Step 3 — Apply v to the seed users to get cycle 2:** v expresses the ratio of cycle₂/cycle₁. So cycle₂ = v × cycle₁ = 0.5 × 2000 = **1000 users**.

The second cycle commences with **1000** additional users.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks. Mark frames this as the 'opposite' of the more common version of the calculation where v is given and GM has to be derived — here you must rearrange the formula. Useful mental model: row 1 of the typical CGM spreadsheet table is your seed (2000); the question asks for the starting value of row 2.

questions.question_text: Uber has already established a very large network of riders and drivers worldwide. Explain how, despite Uber's dominant network, a start-up may still be able to attract participants away from Uber's network. In your answer, be sure to state the general strategic approach that should be employed by the start-up and also give specific examples of actions that could be taken.
questions.model_answer:
**General strategic point (1 mark) — Uber is a network of networks:** Uber is attackable because it isn't one huge homogeneous network — it's a network of networks (broadly, one per city). The network effects across the whole are weaker than its scale would imply, so the network can be undermined by attacking sub-parts. To get full marks, frame your answer around Uber being a network of networks and attackable on that basis.

**Specific example 1 (1 mark) — City-by-city focus:** A start-up could focus on one city and be more attuned to local needs (driver hiring practices, local regulations, payment methods, etc.). Hard for a global incumbent to do well at every locality.

**Specific example 2 (1 mark) — Niche category:** Target one category of users — e.g. luxury cars (Uber's equivalent is 'Uber Black'). Building a superior niche service for one segment is easier than competing across the whole.

**Alternative example — Hard-side attack:** Attack the hard side of the network — the drivers — by giving them better terms (higher take-home, better tools, lower commission).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks total. Mark is explicit: you must frame the answer around Uber being a network of networks to get full marks; just listing tactics without that framing won't reach the top. Specific examples must be tied to Uber, not generic. Examples that earn marks: city-by-city focus, niche category (luxury), or attacking the hard side (drivers) with better terms.

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for Instagram. For each item identified, clearly state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Marking framework:** 6 marks available. Instagram has more than 6 mechanisms, so listing any 6 — correctly named AND briefly described — earns full marks.

**(1) Social Capital CGM (Direct):** Users post content to grow their social standing / following count. The desire for engagement and clout drives more posting and more inviting of friends.

**(2) Organic CGM (Direct):** Word-of-mouth — users tell friends about the platform. Often runs in parallel to the social-capital CGM.

**(3) Network effects — multi-sided (one-sided / two-sided / three-sided depending on framing):** Equivalent marks for: one-sided (users-to-users), two-sided (creators ↔ viewers), or three-sided (users / influencers / advertisers).

**(4) Content-based indirect CGM:** User-generated content shared off-platform (Stories cross-posted, Reels shared elsewhere) drives discovery and re-engagement.

**(5) Ad-space CGM:** The advertising side of the platform — advertiser revenue funds further investment in product, recommendation systems, content moderation, and acquisition.

**(6) Scale-based network effects:** Classic network value increasing with users, plus data scale (more users → better recommendations) and brand scale.

Listing any 6 of these with type clearly named and a brief description gets full marks.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 6 marks. Common ways students lost marks: (a) not naming the CGMs/effects properly, (b) naming them but not describing them — making it hard for the marker to tell whether the student is just listing every CGM they've ever heard of versus actually applying them to Instagram. Each item must be applied to Instagram. Mark notes that students were forewarned by email before the exam that Instagram would feature, so they should have prepared its growth model specifically.

questions.question_text:
At the launch of Meta's Threads product (Meta's competitor to Twitter/X), the company actively encouraged Instagram users to try Threads, and removed friction from the sign-up process by sharing Instagram accounts across both products. Although Instagram and Threads have different uses, Meta's decision effectively resulted in the network relationships between users in Instagram to be replicated in Threads.

On July 6 2023, when Threads was launched, 41.8 million daily active users were reported, which rose to 49.3 million on July 7. But by August 2023, Threads' user activity had decreased to 10.3 million daily active users, down over 79% since the peak, with users spending an average of 3 minutes per day on the platform. This is despite Meta employing intensive A/B testing and iteration to optimise the product's retention performance. Meanwhile, Twitter/X's daily active user count remained more or less constant over that period, with approximately 200 million daily active users, spending, on average, approximately 30 minutes on the platform per day.

With specific reference to relevant concepts studied on the course, provide a reasonable explanation for the user statistics experienced by Threads (and, where relevant, Twitter) over this period. Explain also what strategy the Threads growth team could employ to sustainably grow the daily active users figure again. Comment on how effective this is strategy is likely to be.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Initial boost via Instagram network reuse:** User numbers were initially boosted by reusing the Instagram network — very low friction sign-up. Same situation as the Google+ vs Facebook case study covered in class.

**Point 2 (essentially required) — Sparse network in the new-product context:** The replicated network isn't dense with respect to Threads. People follow others on Instagram for certain reasons (visual content, lifestyle), but Twitter-style discourse is a different use case. Bringing those people over creates a sparse network in Threads — there isn't much content I want to follow because the people I follow on Instagram post for different reasons. This creates anti-network effects with respect to the relevant content type.

**Point 3 — No pull for non-Meta users:** Users not on Instagram, or already on Twitter, have no reason to move to an empty network — there's no real pull beyond the initial onboarding trick.

**Point 4 — Strategy: actively help users build relevant connections:** Encourage users to follow people aligned to their interests (similar to how Twitter's onboarding asks about interests to suggest follows).

**Point 5 — Strategy: surface relevant content (Twitter/TikTok-style):** Recommend content the user might find interesting on a regular basis — they may then follow those creators.

**Point 6 — Strategy: paid influencers:** Pay influencers appropriate to this application space to post on the platform, seeding the kind of content Threads wants.

**Point 7 — Effectiveness commentary:** This will take a long time — effectively rebuilding the network from scratch. The initial onboarding trick doesn't really stick. May also not be effective because many target users have already had a bad first experience, and Twitter users have no compelling reason to move.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 6 marks. Mark says students get marks for any 6 of these points 'as long as point 2 is present' — i.e. the dense-vs-sparse network framing is essentially required. Recognising the parallel to the Google+ vs Facebook case study is the unlock.

questions.question_text: With reference to specific concepts covered on the course, explain why a video-sharing platform-based business that uses shorter-length video content may have an advantage as regards network effects over one that uses relatively long video content.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 (1 mark) — Identify the data-scale network effect:** Recognise this is a data-based network effect question. Shorter videos let the platform gather data about user preferences much more quickly (more videos watched per session = more signal per unit time).

**Point 2 (1 mark) — Explain the mechanism:** Because data is gathered faster, the recommendation/personalisation engine improves faster. Better recommendations attract more users and retain existing ones, which generates more data — a reinforcing data-scale network effect. TikTok is the canonical example of this advantage.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 2 marks. Mark explicitly warns: 'A lot of people answered this question based on things that aren't to do with network effects, and therefore didn't get any marks for this question.' The question says 'with reference to specific concepts covered on the course' and 'as regards network effects' — answers about attention spans, mobile habits, etc. that don't tie back to network effects score zero. 1 mark for naming the concept (data-scale network effect), 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (faster preference-data gathering → faster content tuning).

questions.question_text:
A start-up records the following channel costs in a typical month:

(1)   Cost of Google SEM:  €140000

(2)   Cost of Facebook Ads:  €60000

The start-up also incurs additional costs each month to fully convert potential leads arriving on the above channels.

The start-up acquires, on average, 2000 paying customers per month.

The start-up achieves an average customer Lifetime Value of €600.

If the LTV:CAC ratio must satisfy the typical minimum requirements of potential investors, calculate how much the start-up can afford to spend, on average, per new customer each month on converting channel leads into paying customers.

In your answer, ignore any other business overheads not listed above. Round your final answer to zero decimal places. Do NOT include a € sign in your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Step 1 — Identify the LTV:CAC threshold:** 'Must satisfy the typical minimum requirements of potential investors' means LTV:CAC must be at least **3:1**.

**Step 2 — Calculate the maximum allowable CAC:** With LTV €600, allowable CAC = €600 / 3 = **€200 per customer**.

**Step 3 — Calculate the channel cost per customer:** Total channel costs = €140,000 + €60,000 = €200,000 per month. With 2,000 paying customers per month, channel cost per customer = €200,000 / 2,000 = **€100**.
