**Step 4 — Subtract to find the conversion-cost headroom per customer:** Allowable CAC (€200) − channel cost per customer (€100) = **€100** available to spend on converting channel leads into paying customers.

Final answer: **100**.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Mark stresses the 3:1 LTV:CAC investor minimum is the trigger phrase. Convert monthly aggregate channel costs into per-customer figures using the 2000 customers/month divisor. Final answer is €100 per customer (no € sign, zero decimal places).

questions.question_text: Using concepts studied during the course, discuss the use of ChatGPT and similar tools based on Large Language Models (LLMs) as user acquisition channels. How will these affect the acquisition strategies used by start-ups, and how will they affect existing major digital acquisition channels? Include in your answer one specific technique start-ups could use to improve acquisition performance on LLM-based channels.
questions.model_answer:
**Part A — Effect on existing major digital acquisition channels (~3 marks):** We covered the age of super-aggregation in class. Dominant search channels like Google have become super-aggregators — the point of discovery for all information in a given domain — giving them enormous market power. They aggregate both supply (every product wants to be in their results and adapts its interface accordingly) and demand (marginal cost of adding users is near zero). LLMs threaten to disrupt this status quo because they are likely to become the new point of discovery, sitting one level above the existing super-aggregators. In other words, LLMs risk doing to Google what Google did to news sites and other websites — displacing them as the search/discovery interface. You can also note that Google is responding by adding an LLM layer above its search but hasn't yet figured out how to monetise that.

**Part B — Effect on start-up acquisition strategies (~2 marks):** Start-ups need to recognise that for a period of time there will be a fragmentation of search channels — instead of just Google plus one or two others, multiple LLMs will compete to be the new point of discovery. Start-ups must decide which of those to be active on. The competition may temporarily drive advertising costs down, so start-ups can either reduce budgets or advertise more — but this is likely temporary until a new LLM super-aggregator emerges. They also need to recognise that existing SEO work won't transfer one-to-one: traditional Google SEO rewards inbound links, whereas being surfaced by LLMs depends on appearing in the sources/websites that LLMs are trained on.

**Part C — Specific technique to improve LLM-channel acquisition (1 mark):** Ensure your product is mentioned and recommended in 'best of' guides and similar curated content that LLMs typically index / are trained on.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Common mistake: students saw 'LLM' and answered as if asked 'how can LLMs improve CGMs / content generation' — that is the wrong question and earned few marks. CGMs are NOT mentioned in the question. The question is about LLMs as ACQUISITION CHANNELS. Use course-specific terms: super-aggregation, point of discovery, fragmentation of channels, SEO transferability. ~3 marks for the channel-displacement discussion + ~3 marks split across strategy fragmentation and the specific technique.

questions.question_text: The following cohort activation and retention chart shows the average retention behaviour for a typical cohort of a social media product. Explain the general shape of the graph, and comment on the cohort retention performance of this product.
questions.model_answer:
**Part 1 — Explain the shape (≈2 marks):** The graph falls quickly at first because more users are typically lost during the activation stage — before they have formed a habit around the product. The graph then falls less quickly because users who have formed a habit are less likely to stop using it, so the decay rate reduces. Over a 6-month period (roughly 24 weeks) most users are eventually lost from the product.

**Part 2 — Comment using the social-media context (≈2 marks):** Crucially, the question tells us this is a social-media product. A typical well-performing social-media product would expect to see the chart level off around 60–70% active users after the activation period. This cohort is not turning that corner, so it is under-performing relative to a healthy social-media benchmark.

**Part 3 — Comment on the long-tail retention performance (≈1 mark):** The ongoing retention performance continues to decline. It is not a catastrophic decline — it is slow and steady — but it will ultimately kill the business. There is, however, a reasonable amount of time to experiment and bring the curve up to level terms.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Common errors: (1) only answering one of the two sub-questions, or mixing them together and not fully addressing each; (2) merely DESCRIBING the graph ('retention falls rapidly, then slows') rather than EXPLAINING why it has that shape — description alone earns minimum credit. The marker would award some credit for description but not full marks. Always note the question is worth 5 marks and structure the answer in 5 distinct points. Don't ignore the 'social media' detail — nothing in an exam question is wasted; the 60-70% benchmark is specific to social media.

questions.question_text: In the early days of Linked-In, the corporate social media platform would automatically mail users whenever anyone in a user's network changed any personal information, for example job title or profile picture. As the overall size of the Linked-In network grew, the company decided to discontinue this behaviour. Using concepts covered in the course, discuss why the company initially included the feature, and then later discontinued its use.
questions.model_answer:
**Part 1 — Why the feature was initially included (~1.5 marks):** In the early stage, this was an attempt to increase **engagement intensity** by increasing the **natural frequency** of the product. The emails would bring users back to LinkedIn, and while they were there they might explore further features, invite new users, etc.

**Part 2 — Why it was later discontinued (~1.5 marks):** As the network grew, the feature resulted in too many emails, which would have amounted to **spam**. The frequency of emailing users to re-engage them began to exceed the sustainable natural frequency by too great a margin. This in turn could trigger **anti-network effects** — users associating LinkedIn with annoyance. Additionally, by then there were stronger re-engagement mechanisms available (content written by other users, job notifications, etc.), so the original feature was no longer needed.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: The phrase 'using concepts covered in the course' is critical — answers that don't reference course concepts score poorly or zero. Use the explicit terms: natural frequency, engagement intensity, spam (with some definition), inviting new users, anti-network effects, alternative re-engagement mechanisms. Hitting most of these terms gets full or near-full marks.

questions.question_text: Using network effects concepts studied during the course, state whether Bluesky will eventually have more active users than Twitter/X, and explain the reasons for your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Setup:** A bare opinion earns no marks — you must explain. There is no right or wrong on the eventual outcome (Mark's own guess: no, it won't), so a reasoned answer either way scores full marks if it uses course concepts.

**Sample points (covering both sides):**

**(1) Asymmetry of network types:** Twitter is a multi-sided network, while Bluesky is not yet — note this structural asymmetry.

**(2) Anti-network effects on Twitter:** Twitter currently has active anti-network effects: spam bots, growing distrust of the platform after the takeover, and politicisation. These drive users away and set up reinforcing anti-network effects — an opportunity for Bluesky.

**(3) Bluesky's moderation tooling:** Bluesky has built moderation tools to suppress these anti-network effects, making it a more pleasant environment users can migrate to.

**(4) Sparse network challenge:** Bluesky is initially a sparse network — it is hard to pull users away from Twitter to a less-dense network because network effects are weaker initially.

**(5) Density-acceleration tools:** Bluesky has tried to accelerate network density using tools such as 'follow the people followed by the people you follow' and follow groups.

**(6) Politicisation cuts both ways:** Bluesky is perceived as more left-wing, so right-wing users are unlikely to join, mirroring the inverse effect on Twitter. The polarising stance of Elon Musk creates positive network effects for some users and anti-network effects for others.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Must use network-effects concepts from the course — answers without them score poorly even if interesting. Either conclusion (will / won't overtake) is acceptable provided it is explained with course concepts. Students were notified a week before the exam that Bluesky would feature, so were expected to know the product. Key terms to deploy: multi-sided network, anti-network effects, network density, sparse network, hard-side seeding.

questions.question_text: Explain the concept of subnetwork attack and explain how Bluesky might employ this technique to attract users from Twitter/X to Bluesky.
questions.model_answer:
**Part 1 — Explanation of sub-network attack (≈2 marks):** A sub-network attack exploits the fact that many large networks are in fact networks of smaller networks. In such a situation, the network effects operating across the whole network aren't as powerful as the overall size would suggest — they are weaker within and across sub-networks. It is therefore possible for a start-up to target one or more of these sub-networks and build a superior product experience for users of that specific sub-network, which attracts them to join the new product's network.

**Part 2 — Application to Bluesky vs Twitter/X (≈2 marks):** Twitter is essentially a network of smaller networks, and Bluesky has already had some success attacking the sub-network of users of a particular political persuasion (left-leaning users). Bluesky could continue that strategy for other sub-networks based on particular interest areas. It could also attract key influencers to Bluesky — a hard-side seeding approach — which would in turn attract other users.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Question splits as 2 + 2 marks (definition + application). Use precise course terminology: 'network of networks', weaker network effects within sub-networks, superior product experience for the targeted sub-network, hard-side seeding via influencers.

questions.question_text: For the strategy that you proposed in the previous question, state how effective a strategy of subnetwork attack is likely to be in this case, and explain your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Sample reasoned answer:** The strategy is likely only to be partially effective. Twitter is not a clean network of networks — it does have sub-networks to some extent, but users tend to exist in multiple sub-networks at the same time (news, politics, other interest areas), and the network does not have obvious segmentation in the way that, for example, a geographically segmented network like Uber does. Because of that overlap and lack of clean segmentation, sub-network attack is likely only partially effective.

**Alternative valid answer:** If you argue instead that there is a fairly clean political segmentation that Bluesky can exploit and double down on, that is also a valid answer.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: DEPENDS ON Q10's answer — the marker reads this as a continuation of the strategy proposed in Q10. Don't just repeat what was already written. Need a fairly INSIGHTFUL analysis of why it would or wouldn't work — superficial 'I think this would be very effective' answers earn no marks. Demonstrate mastery of the course concepts (sub-network segmentation, overlap of users across sub-networks, geographical vs interest-based segmentation).

questions.question_text:
A product has a Direct, Social Capital CGM with a cycle-to-cycle sign-up ratio V of 0.5. The growth team runs an experiment where the CGM is changed to a Direct, Financially-Incentivised CGM. In the experiment the referrer and the referred potential new user each receive €5 if the referred potential new user signs up for the start-up's product. When the CGM is initialised with a batch of users, the experiment results in 20% more sign-ups in each cycle of the CGM before it runs to exhaustion, compared to before the change.

Assuming that the average LTV of users is €100, calculate whether this experiment should be fully implemented in the product.

NOTE: Be sure to show your calculation steps.
questions.model_answer:
**Framing:** Both CGMs bring in new users (and thus revenue). The original has no marginal cost (no incentive). The new one brings in more users but incurs cost. Need to compare net revenue.

**Step 1 — Original CGM growth multiplier:** With V = 0.5, GM = 1 / (1 − V) = 1 / 0.5 = **2**. So per starting user, **1 additional new user** is added.

**Step 2 — New CGM's V:** 20% more sign-ups per cycle means V increases by 20%: V_new = 0.5 × 1.20 = **0.6**. (Common error: students added 0.2 to give 0.7 — that's an arithmetic mistake; partial credit still applied if subsequent logic was correct.)

**Step 3 — New CGM growth multiplier:** GM_new = 1 / (1 − 0.6) = **2.5**. So per starting user, **1.5 new users** are added (vs 1 before).

**Step 4 — Cost per new user:** Each new sign-up costs €5 (referrer) + €5 (referred) = **€10 per new user**. For 1.5 new users per starting user, cost = 1.5 × €10 = **€15**.

**Step 5 — Revenue from new users:** New users generate 1.5 × LTV = 1.5 × €100 = **€150**.

**Step 6 — Net earnings per starting user (new CGM):** €150 − €15 = **€135**.

**Step 7 — Compare to original CGM:** Original brings 1 new user × €100 LTV − €0 cost = **€100 net** per starting user.

**Step 8 — Decision:** €135 > €100, so the new CGM generates more net revenue. **The experiment should be fully implemented.**
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Must show working — partial credit follows the logic chain even if a step is wrong. Common arithmetic error: treating '20% more' as +0.2 to V rather than V × 1.2 (so 0.7 instead of 0.6) — still earns most marks if rest is correct. Equivalent approaches accepted: starting with 100 or 1000 users, expressing entirely in revenue terms from the start. Critically, must STATE A CONCLUSION at the end (implement / don't implement) — going through all the calculation but not committing to a position can lose the final mark. The question has appeared in near-identical form in past papers — past-paper practice strongly rewarded.

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for AirBnB. For each item identified, clearly state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Approach:** Same exercise as the main coursework assignment — name the mechanism, state its type clearly, and give a brief description. There are more mechanisms available than there are marks (one mark per correctly identified, named, and described mechanism, up to 8 marks).

**(1) Two-sided network effect — hosts ↔ guests:** Each side becomes more valuable to the other as it grows. More hosts → more places to stay → more guests; more guests → more demand → more hosts list properties.

**(2) Data-scale network effect:** More bookings → better data → better matching, better pricing, better recommendations. The platform's quality improves with use.

**(3) Purchasing-power scale effect:** Larger AirBnB → better unit economics on hosting, payments processing, customer support tooling, etc.

**(4) Brand-scale network effect:** As the network grows, brand recognition makes it easier to acquire new hosts and guests.

**(5) Incentivised CGM — host side:** Referral schemes that reward existing hosts for bringing in new hosts.

**(6) Incentivised CGM — guest side:** Historically AirBnB ran referral credits on the user/guest side as well.

**(7) Organic / social-capital CGM:** Guests share their AirBnB stays on social media, attracting other potential guests.

**(8) Content-based indirect CGM:** Listings themselves are content; SEO drives discovery via search engines.

(Mark indicates the slide showed additional mechanisms beyond what he listed verbally; any further valid mechanisms students named in their answer also scored marks, up to the 8-mark cap.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Students were notified a week before the exam that an Airbnb question would appear. The format mirrors the main course assignment closely. To get the mark for each item you must (a) name the mechanism, (b) state its type clearly, (c) give a brief description of operation. One mark per fully-described mechanism, capped at 8. Mark didn't enumerate every mechanism on his slide — students who identified additional valid mechanisms (e.g. other scale effects, anti-network effects, etc.) also earned marks.

questions.question_text: At one point in its history, Google's founders decided that each director in the business should have up to 100 people directly reporting to them (i.e. with no managers in between) in order to reduce layers of management within the business. This wasn't successful and the decision was later changed to reduce the number of people reporting to each manager. Analyse this situation in the context of the concept of Agency.
questions.model_answer:
**Approach:** Answer in terms of the components of Agency. Reasonable points of view either way score marks; the trick is to address each component explicitly.

**Component 1 — Alignment:** It's difficult for team members to be aligned to the strategy because there's just one manager checking 100 people's work. (You could note it might be partially achievable using tooling — saying both earns marks here.)

**Component 2 — Competence:** Places considerable strain on managers' competence. Suddenly they have 100 reports — an abrupt change; they may previously have managed 10, and they're unlikely to manage 100 effectively. It also requires individual team members to behave more autonomously because they don't have access to their manager. For some employees that works well; others struggle. It only works if people have been invested in to operate autonomously.

**Component 3 — Ownership:** You can argue either direction. Mark's own take: ownership tends to INCREASE because the manager is too busy to own things themselves, so reports must own them. Alternative valid argument: ownership DECREASES because employees have to wait longer for permissions and decisions from the overloaded manager. Both accepted.

**Component 4 — Access to Resources:** Difficult to access management expertise/time because managers are overloaded. But it may be EASIER to access resources in other ways — people who would once have been in entirely different teams are now in the same team, so it may be possible to work more easily with them without management barriers. Alternative view: harder to access other skills because no manager is available to direct you to them. Both accepted.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: If you don't know the components of agency you'll struggle — many students wrote a lot but without referencing the components and scored poorly. Use the components as the structure. Reasonable arguments either way score marks (Mark accepted contradictory positions on ownership and on resource-access). Outlandish, non-credible answers don't score; reasonable points within course concepts do.

questions.question_text:
A founder decides to seek an investment in her start-up. The founder owns 100 million shares out of a total of 150 million total shares prior to the investment. A venture capital firm values the business at $10million prior to any new investment, and offers to a make investment of $5million. A competing investor instead values the business at $12million and offers to make an investment of $8million.

The founder decides to select the investment option with the most favourable outcome for her in terms of the percentage dilution of her shares. Calculate the percentage dilution of her shares after this investment. Express your answer as a fraction.

You must show your calculations and reasoning for full credit.
questions.model_answer:
**Step 1 — Founder's pre-investment proportion:** Founder owns 100M / 150M = **2/3** of the company.

**Step 2 — Investment Option A ($10M valuation, $5M investment):** Investor A's $5M against a $10M pre-money valuation buys 50% of the existing share base. New investor shares = 50% × 150M = 75M new shares, so total shares = 150M + 75M = **225M**. Founder still owns 100M, now of 225M = **4/9**.

**Step 3 — Investment Option B ($12M valuation, $8M investment):** $8M against $12M pre-money = 66.6...% of the existing share base. New shares = 66.6% × 150M = 100M new shares, so total shares = 150M + 100M = **250M**. Founder still owns 100M, now of 250M = **2/5**.

**Step 4 — Compare which is better from a dilution perspective:** 4/9 ≈ 0.444 is bigger than 2/5 = 0.4, so the founder retains more of the company under Option A. Founder chooses **Option A** on dilution grounds.

**Step 5 — Calculate the percentage dilution under the chosen option:** Dilution = (original − new) / original = (2/3 − 4/9) / (2/3) = (6/9 − 4/9) / (6/9) = (2/9) / (6/9) = **1/3**.

Final answer: founder is diluted by **1/3** (one-third).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Same calculation appeared in each of the last two years' papers (with one investment instead of two — the only difference here is comparing two). Numbers are deliberately simple — some students panicked. Marks are awarded along the chain: pre-investment proportion, post-investment proportion under each option, comparison, dilution formula, final fraction. Partial credit is given even with arithmetic slips, as long as logic is followable. Final answer required AS A FRACTION = 1/3. Dilution formula: (original − new) / original.

questions.question_text: Explain why the founder should have chosen the other investment, despite her chosen investment having the better percentage dilution outcome.
questions.model_answer:
**Two points to make (1 mark each):**

**Point 1 — Larger absolute stake despite higher percentage dilution:** Although her share is diluted more in percentage terms under Option B, it is a smaller percentage of a LARGER overall company valuation. Specifically: 2/5 of (12M + 8M) = 2/5 of $20M = $8M (paper value) is bigger than 4/9 of (10M + 5M) = 4/9 of $15M ≈ $6.67M. So on paper she is more well off under Option B. (Caveat: she can't spend any of that until the company exits, but assuming a successful sale or IPO she's in a better position.)

**Point 2 — More cash into the business:** The other investment brings more money into the business, so the company can do more things, or do them faster, and won't have to seek another investment as soon — avoiding more dilution later.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: DEPENDS ON Q15 — this is a follow-up. To get full marks BOTH points must be present (one mark each: the post-money-stake comparison, and the more-money-into-the-business argument). The fact the question is worth 2 marks should signal there are two distinct points to make.

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for ChatGPT. For each item identified, clearly state its type and provide a brief description of its operation in the context of ChatGPT.
questions.model_answer:
**Marking framework:** 6 marks available. ChatGPT has more than 6 mechanisms / effects, so listing any 6 — correctly named AND briefly described in the ChatGPT context — earns full marks.

**(1) Direct Organic CGM (1 mark):** Word-of-mouth was the dominant early growth engine — every conversation that surprised a user (Nov 2022 launch) acted as a referral event, driving the famous 100M-users-in-2-months curve.

**(2) Indirect Content CGM — initially company-generated, now user-generated (1 mark):** OpenAI demos and screenshots of impressive answers circulated heavily on X / Reddit / TikTok. Initially OpenAI-amplified (CG); now overwhelmingly user-shared screenshots and prompt libraries (UG) — the textbook CG → UG transition.

**(3) Data network effect / RLHF learning loop (1 mark):** More usage → more thumbs-up/down and preference data → better fine-tuned model → better answers attract / retain more users. Logan frames this as a learning loop with network-effect-like compounding properties; it is ChatGPT's strongest moat-like mechanism.

**(4) Scale-based network effects (data + brand) (1 mark):** Scale of training data, infrastructure cost amortisation, and brand recognition all compound with usage — small competitors cannot match the inference cost-curve or brand at the same scale.

**(5) Two-sided developer / plugin / GPTs network effect (1 mark):** Custom GPTs and the GPT Store create a soft two-sided effect: more users → more incentive for developers to build custom GPTs → more useful product → more users. Weaker than classical social NEs but real.

**(6) Ad-space / monetisation CGM via paid tiers (1 mark):** ChatGPT Plus / Enterprise revenue funds further model investment (more compute, better RLHF pipelines, more researchers), which improves the product, which acquires more users — a self-funding compounding loop similar to an ad-space CGM but powered by subscription revenue.

Alternative items that also earn credit if listed instead: Direct Invitation CGM (referral/share-link in Team/Enterprise), Workflow-embedding retention loop (not strictly a CGM but creditable as a compounding mechanism). Listing any 6 of the above with type clearly named and a ChatGPT-specific description gets full marks.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 6 marks, 1 per mechanism. Mark requires both correct naming (using exact taxonomy: Direct Organic CGM, Indirect Content CGM, data network effect, scale network effect, two-sided NE, ad-space / revenue-funded CGM) AND a brief description applied to ChatGPT specifically — generic descriptions of the mechanism without ChatGPT context lose half a mark. Common errors: (a) confusing the data flywheel with a classical network effect (Logan accepts data-NE / learning-loop, but candidates should not claim 'more users makes the chat better for me' — that's wrong); (b) listing 'AI moat' or 'first-mover advantage' which are not course-taxonomy items and earn nothing; (c) describing a mechanism without naming its type. Forewarn: ChatGPT was flagged as an exam product, so candidates should have prepared this growth model.

questions.question_text: ChatGPT reportedly reached around 100 million users in roughly two months after its November 2022 launch — the fastest consumer-product growth ever recorded — despite OpenAI spending almost nothing on paid acquisition during that period. Identify the dominant compounding growth mechanism responsible for this curve, and explain how it operated. Identify one secondary CGM that supported it, and explain how that secondary CGM compounded the effect.
questions.model_answer:
**Part A — Dominant CGM (2 marks):**

The dominant mechanism was a **Direct Organic CGM** — word-of-mouth referrals (1 mark). Each conversation that produced a surprisingly good answer (writing, code, planning) effectively acted as a referral event: users told friends, family and colleagues to 'try this', without any invitation link, code or paid incentive (1 mark). The fact that OpenAI was not running paid acquisition is a textbook organic-CGM signature — the exponential rise in homepage traffic with no corresponding ad spend is exactly Logan's stated detection method for organic CGMs.

**Part B — Secondary CGM (2 marks):**

The secondary mechanism was an **Indirect Content CGM**, content-based (1 mark). Screenshots of impressive ChatGPT outputs — code, essays, creative answers — circulated heavily on X, Reddit and TikTok. Initially this was company-amplified (OpenAI demos), but it rapidly became user-generated (UG) (1 mark). Crucially, this content compounded the organic CGM by operating **above** the ChatGPT transaction frequency — even users who weren't actively using ChatGPT that week were repeatedly reminded it existed via screenshots in their social feeds, which reduced churn and pulled lapsed users back, while also acting as discovery for non-users.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming Direct Organic CGM (must use the taxonomy term, not just 'word of mouth'); 1 mark for explaining the no-paid-acquisition / exponential-traffic-without-ad-spend signature; 1 mark for naming Indirect Content CGM (or Content-based Indirect CGM); 1 mark for explaining the screenshot mechanism with reference either to the CG → UG transition OR to operating above transaction frequency. Common errors: (a) calling it a 'viral loop' generically without naming the CGM type — half marks; (b) confusing this with a network effect — explicitly wrong, the question asks for CGMs; (c) naming the data flywheel as the dominant mechanism — wrong because the data flywheel doesn't acquire users, it improves the product. Distinct from paper2025_q2 which asks about LLMs as acquisition channels for *other* startups; this asks about ChatGPT's *own* growth.

questions.question_text: A common student claim is that ChatGPT benefits from strong network effects in the same way that products like Instagram or Snapchat do. Using concepts covered on the course, explain why this claim is largely incorrect for classical network effects, and explain what compounding effect ChatGPT does benefit from instead. Comment on whether this effect provides a defensible moat against competitors such as Anthropic's Claude or Google's Gemini.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Classical NEs are weak for ChatGPT (1 mark):** A classical direct network effect requires that other users on the product make the product more valuable to me. For ChatGPT this is largely absent — the value of my next conversation does not depend on whether 1 million or 100 million other people are also using ChatGPT. Unlike Snapchat (where I need my friends on the network) or Instagram (where I need creators and audience), ChatGPT's per-user utility is essentially independent of co-users.

**Point 2 — The actual effect is a data network effect / RLHF learning loop (1 mark):** What ChatGPT does benefit from is a **data-scale network effect**, very similar in structure to TikTok's. More usage produces more interactions, more thumbs-up/down feedback, and more RLHF preference data. That data is used to fine-tune subsequent model versions, producing better answers, which attracts and retains more users, which produces more data — a reinforcing data-scale loop. Logan accepts this framing as a *learning loop* with NE-like compounding properties.

**Point 3 — Mechanism in ChatGPT specifically (1 mark):** Each conversation generates implicit and explicit signal: thumbs ratings, regenerations, edits, abandonment. This signal quality scales with raw usage; it is genuinely hard for a smaller competitor to replicate without comparable traffic. Combined with scale-based effects (training compute, infrastructure cost amortisation) the loop is real.

**Point 4 — Moat commentary (1 mark):** However, the moat is weaker than classical NEs against competitors like Claude or Gemini for two reasons: (a) base-model capability gains are increasingly driven by pre-training scale and architecture, not RLHF data — competitors with comparable compute can leapfrog without ChatGPT's data; (b) switching cost for users is essentially zero (no friend graph to lose), so a meaningfully better competitor product can take share quickly. The data-NE provides an advantage but not the lock-in that, e.g., Snapchat enjoys.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for stating classical direct NE is weak/absent and saying why (per-user utility independent of co-users); 1 mark for naming the data-scale network effect / learning loop; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism in ChatGPT specifically (RLHF, thumbs, fine-tuning); 1 mark for the moat commentary — must say the moat is weaker than classical NEs and give at least one reason (zero switching cost, pre-training-driven gains, or competitor compute parity). Common errors: (a) claiming ChatGPT has strong classical NEs because 'lots of people use it' — wrong, that is scale, not NE; (b) describing the data flywheel without naming the data network effect taxonomy term; (c) declaring it an unassailable moat — Logan deducts for over-claiming.

questions.question_text: Internal data at OpenAI suggests that ChatGPT users who do not get a useful answer from the product within their first one or two sessions almost always churn within a week, while users who do get a useful answer in those early sessions show monthly retention of around 80%. Using concepts covered on the course, identify what this gap represents, describe what the 'activation moment' for ChatGPT most likely is, and suggest two product interventions the growth team could deploy to close this gap.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Identify the gap (1 mark):** The gap between near-100% early churn for non-activated users and ~80% retention for activated users is a textbook example of **activation inequality** — the very large performance difference between cohorts who pass the activation event and those who do not. It tells the growth team that retention work is dominated by activation work: if the user fails to activate, no amount of downstream lifecycle messaging will save them.

**Point 2 — Identify the activation moment (1 mark):** ChatGPT's activation moment is the **first response that produces a genuinely useful answer for the user's actual job** — typically writing, code, summarisation, or planning. It is not simply 'sent first message' (too shallow) and not '7-day-active' (too late). The moment is task-completion-flavoured: the user got something out of the product they couldn't easily get elsewhere.

**Point 3 — Intervention 1 — onboarding to a high-quality first task (1 mark):** Replace the empty-textbox cold-start with an onboarding flow that asks the user what they want to do (write an email, debug code, plan a trip), then routes them to a templated prompt known to produce a high-quality answer for that intent. This raises the probability of a useful first response and shortens time-to-activation.

**Point 4 — Intervention 2 — second-session re-engagement around workflow embedding (1 mark):** For users who completed one useful task, prompt the second session around a recurring workflow ('most users come back to draft weekly emails / plan their week / fix code') so that activation extends into habit formation. ChatGPT's retention story is workflow embedding rather than classical NE, so the activation event must hand over cleanly into a recurring use-case before the user drops off. Acceptable alternatives: example-prompt galleries, custom-GPT recommendations matched to declared intent, in-product nudges to save useful conversations as templates.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming activation inequality (the taxonomy term — 'big gap between activated and non-activated cohorts' is also creditable but weaker); 1 mark for a credible, ChatGPT-specific activation moment definition (must be task-utility flavoured, not just 'sent a message'); 1 mark for each of two distinct, plausible interventions tied to either time-to-first-useful-answer OR workflow embedding. Generic interventions like 'send a welcome email' or 'improve UX' score zero unless explicitly tied to activation. Common errors: confusing activation with retention; defining the activation moment as a vanity metric (account creation, first message); proposing only one intervention.

questions.question_text: ChatGPT does not have an obvious 'natural' transaction frequency in the way Deliveroo (4 orders every 28 days) or Snapchat (daily messaging) do. Using concepts covered in the course, propose a plausible natural-frequency / NaP framing for ChatGPT and justify it. Comment briefly on why this NaP is harder to set than for those other products.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Propose a NaP (1 mark):** A defensible NaP for ChatGPT is **'3 useful responses per week' (3r7)** for the general consumer, or equivalently **'sessions per workday' (e.g. 1s1 or 2s1)** for productivity / professional use. Both encode workflow embedding at roughly weekly cadence.

**Point 2 — Justify in course terms (1 mark):** The justification is **workflow embedding** — ChatGPT's retention is driven by users incorporating it into a recurring task (drafting weekly emails, weekly planning, code-debugging during the working week). The NaP must therefore match the cadence of the underlying task; weekly is a defensible floor because most professional workflows have a weekly rhythm. A daily NaP overshoots typical use; a monthly NaP undershoots — the user would never form a habit at that cadence and would churn.

**Point 3 — Why NaP is harder to set here (1 mark):** Unlike Deliveroo (where ordering food *is* the transaction and the cadence is observable) or Snapchat (where messaging frequency is intrinsic to the product), ChatGPT covers many heterogeneous use-cases — code, writing, learning, planning — each with a different natural cadence. There is no single transaction; the 'transaction' is whatever recurring task the user embeds it into. So NaP varies meaningfully by user segment, and a single company-wide NaP is a coarse approximation. Companies handle this by segmenting users and tracking segment-specific natural frequencies.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for proposing a credible NaP (must use a cadence form, e.g. NrP or NsP — '3 useful responses per week', 'one session per workday' — vague answers like 'often' score zero); 1 mark for justifying it via workflow embedding or comparable course concept; 1 mark for the harder-to-set commentary, which must mention heterogeneous use-cases or absence of an intrinsic single transaction. Common errors: proposing 'DAU' as a NaP (too generic — DAU is not a NaP); not anchoring the justification in workflow-embedding / habit-formation language.

questions.question_text:
ChatGPT's user growth was explosive between November 2022 and mid-2023, but visibly decelerated through late 2023 and 2024. Around the same period, OpenAI shifted significant strategic attention from pure consumer growth toward enterprise / API revenue (ChatGPT Enterprise, Team, and developer platform).

(a) Using concepts covered on the course, explain why the consumer-side growth curve decelerated.

(b) Explain why a B2C-led product like ChatGPT might deliberately pivot resources toward B2B / enterprise and what risks this transition carries.
questions.model_answer:
**Part (a) — Why consumer growth decelerated (2 marks):**

**(i) Saturation of the organic CGM (1 mark):** The Direct Organic CGM that fuelled the 100M-in-2-months curve has a finite seed pool — once most early-adopter and curious-user clusters have heard about ChatGPT through word-of-mouth and screenshots, the organic referral coefficient v decays toward zero. By definition, the growth multiplier GM = 1/(1−v) collapses toward 1 (no further amplification), and continued growth must come from linear marketing or new CGMs. Logan calls this 'linear-marketing saturation' / CGM exhaustion.

**(ii) Competitive fragmentation (1 mark):** Alternative products (Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, Meta AI, Perplexity) entered the same point-of-discovery space. Because switching cost in ChatGPT is essentially zero (no social graph, no embedded data) some users diverted to alternatives, and some new users went straight to competitors. The single-winner LLM market that the early curve implied did not materialise.

**Part (b) — Pivot to B2B and its risks (3 marks):**

**(iii) Reasons for the pivot — economics and CGM type (1 mark):** B2B / enterprise contracts have far higher LTV, longer retention, and meaningful switching costs (data integrations, custom GPTs, security review, procurement contracts). Also, an enterprise rollout effectively gives OpenAI an *invitation CGM* — once a company adopts ChatGPT Enterprise, employees are onboarded en masse, which is much more efficient than per-user consumer acquisition.

**(iv) Reason — funding the data flywheel (1 mark):** Enterprise revenue funds the compute and research investment that keeps the underlying model ahead — i.e. it powers the revenue-funded CGM (similar to an ad-space CGM) that compounds back into consumer-side product quality. Without enterprise revenue, OpenAI cannot fund the next training run.

**(v) Risk — organisational and product mismatch (1 mark):** B2B and B2C products require different organisations: enterprise sales, security/compliance, account management vs. consumer growth/product-marketing. Logan's organisational point applies — running both well from the same org is hard, and the consumer experience can degrade if the product becomes optimised for enterprise admin features. There is also reputational risk: if ChatGPT is perceived primarily as an enterprise tool, the consumer organic CGM may weaken further. Acceptable alternative risks: dependence on a small number of large contracts (concentration risk); slower iteration cycle imposed by enterprise procurement.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Two-part question — both parts must be answered. Part (a): 1 mark for organic CGM saturation / linear-marketing saturation (must reference CGM exhaustion or v → 0); 1 mark for competitive fragmentation / zero switching cost. Part (b): 1 mark for an LTV / invitation-CGM rationale tied to enterprise economics; 1 mark for revenue-funds-the-flywheel point; 1 mark for an organisational or reputational risk that names the course concept (org mismatch, concentration, consumer-side erosion). Logan explicitly flags this two-part angle ('why did ChatGPT grow so fast AND why has growth slowed') in revision; missing part (b) is the common failure. Don't accept generic 'AI hype faded' — must be expressed in CGM / network terms.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Two-part question — both parts must be answered. Watch for (a) saturation AND (b) pivot-rationale; missing either part loses substantial marks.

questions.question_text: A small UK-based start-up wants to compete with ChatGPT in the consumer LLM-assistant market. Despite OpenAI's enormous lead in users, brand and compute, you have been asked to advise the start-up on how it could realistically attract users away from ChatGPT. Using concepts covered on the course, propose a general strategic approach and give two specific, plausible tactical examples that follow from that approach. Comment briefly on the role of open-source models in this attack.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — General strategic approach (1 mark):** ChatGPT, despite its scale, is attackable on the same logic Logan applies to Uber: it is not a monolithic dense network but more like a **collection of weakly-coupled use-case sub-networks** (writing, coding, learning, planning, role-play, etc.) with **near-zero switching cost** (no friend graph, minimal data lock-in). Therefore the right approach is **niche / sub-network attack** — build a clearly superior product for one use-case, not a worse-everywhere general competitor.

**Point 2 — Specific tactic 1 — niche vertical product (1 mark):** Pick one underserved vertical — e.g. an LLM assistant tightly integrated into a UK-specific developer toolchain, or a tutoring assistant aligned to UK A-Level / SQA syllabuses. Build deeper-than-ChatGPT integration and curriculum/codebase awareness in that vertical. Users who do that one task often will switch for the better experience, exactly because switching cost is zero.

**Point 3 — Specific tactic 2 — privacy / data-handling angle (1 mark):** Attack on a dimension OpenAI cannot easily match: on-device or fully-private inference, no training on user data, EU/UK data-residency, or open-weight model bring-your-own-key. This appeals to a specific user segment (regulated professions, privacy-conscious users) and is hard for the incumbent to mirror without cannibalising its own data flywheel. Alternative creditable tactic: hard-side seeding via paying expert contributors / reviewers to fine-tune a domain-specific model.

**Point 4 — Role of open-source (1 mark):** Open-source / open-weight base models (Llama-class, Mistral-class) materially lower the cost of entry — the start-up no longer has to fund a frontier pre-training run, only fine-tuning and product-layer work. This collapses the scale-based moat and enables niche attacks at viable economics; it does not erase ChatGPT's data-NE / RLHF advantage at the frontier, but it makes the niche-attack strategy economically realistic where it would otherwise be impossible.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for a strategic approach explicitly framed as niche / sub-network attack on a weakly-coupled-network incumbent (must reference the network-of-networks / sub-network or zero-switching-cost framing — Logan deducts for tactics-without-strategy answers, exactly as in paper2024_q12); 1 mark for each of two distinct, plausible tactics tied to that strategy; 1 mark for an open-source commentary that mentions cost-of-entry collapse OR moat-erosion. Common errors: (a) suggesting generic 'better marketing' or 'cheaper price' without strategic framing — minimal credit; (b) naming three tactics but no strategy — half marks; (c) ignoring the open-source part.

questions.question_text: Compare and contrast the activation moments of ChatGPT and Snapchat. In each case, name the activation moment in one short phrase and explain in one sentence why activation inequality is severe for that product.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — ChatGPT (1 mark):** Activation moment = **first response that produces a genuinely useful answer for the user's actual job** (writing, code, planning). Activation inequality is severe because there is no social graph to anchor the user; if the first one or two sessions don't produce utility, the user has no reason to return and churns within a week, while activated users hit ~80% monthly retention.

**Point 2 — Snapchat (1 mark):** Activation moment = **sending a snap and receiving a reciprocal snap from a friend** (time-to-first-reciprocal-snap). Activation inequality is severe because the product's value is the social loop — without a reciprocating friend the network is empty and the user churns within days, whereas activated users sit on the social-media ~60% retention floor.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per product. Each mark requires (i) a correctly framed activation moment — task-utility for ChatGPT, reciprocal-snap for Snapchat; (ii) a one-sentence justification of activation inequality that names the underlying mechanism (workflow embedding for ChatGPT, social loop for Snapchat). Half-credit if the activation moment is named but the inequality justification is missing or generic. Common errors: defining ChatGPT activation as 'first message sent' (too shallow) or Snapchat activation as 'account created' (vanity metric).

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for Deliveroo (or food delivery generally — Uber Eats, Meituan are equivalent). For each item identified, clearly state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Approach:** Same exercise as the AirBnB / Instagram inventory questions in past papers — name the mechanism, state its type clearly, and give a brief description tied specifically to food delivery. There are more mechanisms available than there are marks (one mark per correctly identified, named, and described mechanism, up to 8 marks).

**(1) Three-sided network effect — diners ↔ restaurants ↔ riders (1 mark):** Each side becomes more valuable to the others as it grows. More diners → more restaurants want to list → more selection → more diners. More riders → faster delivery → more diners. The atomic network is **the city** — London diners don't benefit from Tokyo restaurant supply.

**(2) Direct invitation CGM — refer-a-friend codes (1 mark):** Both Deliveroo and Uber Eats run classic referral schemes where existing users get credit for inviting new users (and the new user gets a discount on their first order). A direct, financially-incentivised CGM.

**(3) Indirect content / social-capital CGM — weak (1 mark):** Some social sharing of orders (e.g. Instagram stories of meals), but weak relative to the invitation CGM. Worth naming and noting its limited contribution.

**(4) Data-scale network effect — demand forecasting and dispatch (1 mark):** More orders → better data on rider routing, restaurant prep times, and demand spikes → faster, cheaper, more reliable delivery. The platform's operational quality improves with use.

**(5) Local-liquidity flywheel (1 mark):** Within a city, density compounds — more orders per square kilometre means a rider can chain deliveries, lowering cost per order and unlocking lower minimum-spend thresholds, which attracts more diners. A geographically constrained scale effect.

**(6) Brand-scale network effect (1 mark):** As the network grows, brand recognition lowers acquisition friction — diners default to the most-recognised app when ordering, restaurants treat being listed as table stakes, riders sign up with the leading platform first.

**(7) Purchasing-power scale effect (1 mark):** A larger Deliveroo gets better unit economics on payments processing, customer-support tooling, packaging deals, and corporate-account contracts.

**(8) Habit-formation loop around the NaP (1 mark):** Once a diner hits the 4o28 cadence (4 orders every 28 days), the product is embedded in the weekly routine, increasing retention and reducing reliance on paid re-acquisition.

**Honest caveat (no mark, but expected at the top of a strong answer):** Most growth in food delivery is **paid linear marketing**, not compounding. The mechanisms above exist but the invitation CGM is weak and a lot of acquisition is TV / Google / social ads. A top answer flags this distinction explicitly.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 8 marks. One mark per correctly identified mechanism that is (a) named, (b) typed clearly, and (c) briefly described as it applies to food delivery. There are more than 8 mechanisms available — students who identify any 8 valid mechanisms score full marks. Watch for the common failure mode of listing every CGM the student has ever heard of without applying it to food delivery (cf. paper2024_q13 marking notes on Instagram). Bonus credit (within the cap) for the candid linear-marketing-vs-compounding caveat — Mark Logan flags this distinction as a key honest framing for food delivery.

questions.question_text: Identify the principal Compounding Growth Mechanism (CGM) used by Deliveroo and Uber Eats. Then explain why most of these companies' user growth should NOT be classified as a CGM, despite their large advertising spend. Use specific course terminology in your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**Part 1 — Principal CGM (1 mark):** The principal CGM is a **Direct, Financially-Incentivised (Invitation) CGM** — refer-a-friend codes where the referrer and the referred new user both receive credit on their next order. Identical in form to the Uber referral scheme covered in class.

**Part 2 — Why most growth is NOT a CGM (1 mark):** A CGM by definition is *compounding* — the output of one cycle becomes the input of the next, and growth is generated by users themselves. The bulk of Deliveroo / Uber Eats user acquisition comes from **paid acquisition channels** — TV, Google SEM, Facebook ads, billboards, sponsored content. These are **linear marketing**: spend €X this month, get Y customers; spend nothing next month, get nothing. There is no cycle-to-cycle multiplier.

**Part 3 — Course-terminology framing (2 marks):** The distinction matters because (a) **growth multiplier GM = 1 / (1 − V)** only applies to the genuinely compounding portion of acquisition; the linear-marketing portion is just a fixed input each cycle, not a multiplier (1 mark). (b) Honest growth-modelling for food delivery therefore decomposes monthly new-customer numbers into a small invitation-CGM contribution and a much larger linear-marketing contribution, and the LTV:CAC test must be applied to the linear-marketing portion specifically — it is the dominant cost (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks split 1 + 1 + 2. The phrase 'most of these companies' growth should NOT be classified as a CGM' is the trigger for the linear-marketing distinction — students who simply describe the referral scheme without addressing the linear-marketing point cap at 2 marks. Specific terms expected: invitation CGM (or financially-incentivised CGM), linear marketing, growth multiplier / GM = 1/(1−V), cycle-to-cycle multiplier, LTV:CAC. Mark Logan flags this as one of the harder CGM-vs-linear-marketing distinctions in the course.

questions.question_text: Deliveroo's network effects are three-sided (diners ↔ restaurants ↔ riders) but geographically local. Using course concepts, explain why a national TV-advertising campaign launched before a city has reached sufficient liquidity is likely to waste money. What strategy should be used instead?
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Atomic network in food delivery is the city, not the nation (1 mark):** Network value for a diner depends on the density of restaurants and riders **in their own postcode**, not nationally. A diner in Aberdeen does not benefit from Deliveroo having a strong network in London. The atomic network — the smallest unit at which the product is meaningfully useful — is the city (or even sub-city catchment).

**Point 2 — National advertising into a sparse local network burns money (1 mark):** A TV ad seen by viewers in cities where restaurant selection is thin and rider supply is patchy will drive sign-ups whose **first experience is a bad one** — long waits, limited menu, cold food. These users churn immediately, and because activation in food delivery is unrecoverable for many users (the first failure kills them), the marketing spend is largely wasted. This is the **sparse network** problem applied to acquisition spend.

**Point 3 — Correct strategy: city-by-city saturation, then expand (2 marks):** Launch and saturate one city at a time — concentrate marketing spend, restaurant onboarding, and rider seeding within a single geography until liquidity is achieved (1 mark). Only then move to the next city, and only switch on broader-reach channels (national TV, brand ads) once enough cities are individually dense enough that a typical viewer's local network can deliver a good first-order experience. This is the canonical **atomic-network growth pattern** Mark Logan emphasises — exactly what Snapchat did with high-school cohorts and what Uber did city-by-city (1 mark).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks split 1 + 1 + 2. Required terminology: atomic network, sparse network (or 'sparse-locally'), liquidity, city-by-city. The unrecoverable-first-failure point earns marks under either point 2 or point 3. A common failure mode is to argue 'national ads are expensive' without invoking atomic-network / sparse-network concepts — that style of answer caps at 1 mark.

questions.question_text: On Deliveroo, the activation event is a first order delivered hot, on time, and correct. Industry data suggests that for many users, a single failed first order (cold food, missing items, late delivery) results in permanent churn — the user uninstalls or never returns. Using course concepts, explain why activation in food delivery exhibits especially severe activation inequality, and identify two operational levers Deliveroo can pull to protect first-order outcomes.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Define activation inequality in this context (1 mark):** Activation inequality describes the gap between what activated users do (high retention, repeat orders, eventually reaching the 4o28 NaP) and what non-activated users do (churn within days). For food delivery the gap is unusually severe because the first-order experience is a **physical, real-world event** with many failure modes — temperature, accuracy, timing, packaging, rider behaviour — any one of which can ruin the experience.

**Point 2 — First-failure unrecoverability (1 mark):** Unlike a software product where a confused first session can be salvaged by an in-app tooltip or a follow-up email, a cold-food failure is a **lived bad experience** the user remembers viscerally. Many users will not give the platform a second chance — the first failure is unrecoverable. This makes the activation funnel binary: succeed once, retain at high rates; fail once, lose forever.

**Point 3 — Operational lever 1: rider density and dispatch quality (1 mark):** Ensuring rider supply is sufficient in the user's catchment area at the moment of order — typically by paying riders an hourly minimum during off-peak periods, by surge incentives at peaks, and by routing algorithms that minimise pickup-to-drop-off time — directly reduces late deliveries (the most common failure mode).

**Point 4 — Operational lever 2: restaurant quality / accuracy controls (1 mark):** Onboarding restaurants with prep-time discipline, packaging standards, and order-accuracy SLAs; suspending or de-ranking restaurants whose error rate exceeds a threshold; subsidising tamper-proof / insulated packaging. Either of these — or related levers like proactive refunds for failed first orders, generous first-order refund policy to convert a near-miss into a recovered user — earns the second-lever mark.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks split 1 + 1 + 1 + 1. The phrase 'activation inequality' must be deployed (point 1). 'Operations is the activation function' framing (from cribsheet) is acceptable shorthand for points 3 and 4. Either of the two operational levers in point 4 — or any other plausible operational lever (proactive refunds, first-order quality guarantees, geographic rollout discipline) — earns the mark, provided it is tied to a specific failure mode. Generic 'improve customer service' answers do not earn the lever marks.

questions.question_text: Deliveroo has publicly stated its Natural act of Product (NaP) as '4 orders every 28 days' (4o28). Explain what this NaP means, and discuss why this particular cadence is an appropriate retention metric for a food-delivery product (as opposed to, say, a daily or weekly NaP).
questions.model_answer:
**Part 1 — What 4o28 means (1 mark):** 4o28 is the threshold of repeated product use that defines a **retained, habituated user**. A diner who places at least 4 orders in any rolling 28-day window has, on Deliveroo's data, embedded the product in their routine and is highly likely to keep ordering; a diner below that cadence is in the activation / re-activation funnel and at risk of churn. The NaP is the operational target the growth team uses to define 'activated' for cohort analysis.

**Part 2 — Why a roughly weekly cadence fits food delivery (1 mark):** Food delivery is a **transactional, paid-per-use product**. Daily would be unrealistic because most users cook, eat at work, or eat out for most meals — daily ordering would only describe a tiny segment of high-spending users and would set the activation bar so high that most genuinely retained users would be classified as churned. Weekly (1 order / 7 days = 4 / 28) matches the realistic upper end of normal household usage.

**Part 3 — Why not slower than weekly (1 mark):** A monthly or less-frequent NaP would be too slow to detect churn in time to intervene. By the time a user had failed to order for 60 days you would already have lost them. The 28-day window is short enough to flag at-risk users while remaining realistic — the cadence corresponds to the natural rhythm of a habituated household using the product roughly once a week.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks split 1 + 1 + 1. Mark Logan's lecture explicitly cites 4o28 as Deliveroo's stated NaP — students should memorise the number and reference it explicitly. Acceptable variations on point 2/3: arguing the cadence matches the underlying transactional frequency (people don't order takeaway every day), arguing the window is short enough for early-warning churn detection, arguing it corresponds to habit-formation thresholds. Answers that fail to name the 4o28 figure or fail to justify the cadence cap at 1 mark.

questions.question_text: When launching a new city, Deliveroo faces a classic chicken-and-egg problem: diners won't order without restaurant selection and reliable riders; restaurants won't list without diner volume; riders won't sign up without orders to fulfil. (a) Identify the hard side of this three-sided market and explain how Deliveroo solved the seeding problem at city launch. (b) Identify two distinct things that can go wrong with this seeding strategy.
questions.model_answer:
**Part (a) — Identify the hard side and the seeding solution (2 marks):**

**The hard side is the riders (1 mark):** In a three-sided food-delivery market the supply side that is hardest to recruit cold-start is the riders — restaurants will list opportunistically because listing is low-cost, and diners will try the app for a discount, but riders need *paid hours* to be willing to show up. Without riders, no orders can be fulfilled and the other two sides see immediate failure.

**Solution — pay riders an hourly minimum during launch (1 mark):** Deliveroo seeded rider supply by paying an hourly minimum (rather than purely per-delivery rates) during the launch phase of a new city. This guaranteed riders enough income to show up even when order volume was thin, ensuring delivery was reliable from day one. Once order volume crossed a liquidity threshold the hourly minimum could be tapered and rider pay reverted to a per-delivery model. With reliable supply on the rider side, restaurant onboarding and diner acquisition follow more easily.

**Part (b) — Two things that can go wrong (3 marks):**

**Failure 1 — Cost overrun if liquidity isn't reached fast enough (1 mark):** The hourly minimum is a subsidy — every rider-hour without an order is a direct loss. If demand seeding (paid marketing, restaurant onboarding) doesn't catch up quickly enough, the per-city launch budget is consumed before liquidity tips and the city runs unprofitably for far longer than planned. Multiplied across many cities this can sink the business.

**Failure 2 — Rider quality / churn problems when the subsidy is removed (1 mark):** Riders who joined for the guaranteed hourly rate may quit or reduce hours when the platform switches to per-delivery pay, causing a supply collapse just as you need stable supply to support growing demand. This can produce a sudden activation-killing spike in late deliveries.

**Failure 3 (alternative for the third mark) — Anti-network effects on the demand side from poor early experiences (1 mark):** If launch is attempted before rider supply is genuinely seeded, early diners hit the unrecoverable-first-failure problem (cold food, late delivery) and the local market is poisoned — re-launching the same city later is harder than launching it fresh, because the local population has already had a bad experience. (Other valid answers: regulatory backlash from gig-economy controversies; restaurant exclusivity wars with Uber Eats / Just Eat squeezing margins; rider subsidy creates a precedent that's politically hard to remove.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 5 marks split 2 (part a: 1 for naming the hard side + 1 for the hourly-minimum mechanism) + 3 (part b: 1 mark each for any two distinct failure modes; the third mark is for either depth on those two failures or a third distinct failure). Required terminology: hard side, chicken-and-egg, seeding, liquidity threshold. The hourly-minimum-pay mechanism is the cribsheet-flagged answer for the seeding question — students who guess 'discount diners first' on the hard-side question lose the seeding mark. Acceptable failure modes: cost overrun, rider churn at subsidy removal, demand-side poisoning from premature launch, regulatory backlash, restaurant exclusivity costs.

questions.question_text: Deliveroo and Uber Eats already operate large networks across most major UK cities. Explain how a well-funded start-up could nevertheless attack Deliveroo's network in a single city (e.g. Glasgow). State the general strategic approach, and give two specific tactical examples a Glasgow-based start-up could employ. Comment briefly on how effective this approach is likely to be.
questions.model_answer:
**General strategic point — Deliveroo is a network of networks (1 mark):** Deliveroo's network is geographically segmented — the atomic network is the city, and there are no meaningful network effects spanning Glasgow and London. A Glasgow start-up does not need to compete with Deliveroo's national scale; it only needs to build a *denser, better-experienced* sub-network within Glasgow. The framing 'Deliveroo is a network of networks, attackable on that basis' is the unlock — same logic Mark Logan applies to Uber in the 2024 paper.

**Tactical example 1 — Hard-side attack on riders (1 mark):** Offer Glasgow riders better terms — higher per-delivery rates, lower commission, an hourly minimum during the launch period, better app tooling, faster payout cycles. Riders are the hard side of the market; pulling rider supply out of Deliveroo into your platform reduces Deliveroo's local liquidity and improves yours simultaneously.

**Tactical example 2 — Niche / category attack (1 mark):** Target a Glasgow-specific segment Deliveroo serves poorly — e.g. exclusive partnerships with independent Glasgow restaurants Deliveroo's commission rates have priced out, or a category like late-night / student-area delivery, or a halal-only / vegan-only sub-product. Build a clearly superior product experience for that sub-network so it tips locally.

**Effectiveness commentary (2 marks):** This is likely to be **partially effective in Glasgow specifically** but very hard to scale beyond it (1 mark). City-by-city beachheads are real (the Uber-vs-local-incumbent pattern Logan teaches), and Deliveroo's national marketing economics don't help inside a single city — the local startup can match or beat unit economics within its beachhead. However, two structural constraints limit upside (1 mark): (i) Deliveroo can respond *within Glasgow* by subsidising rider pay and restaurant commissions in that one city until the start-up runs out of money — incumbents can ringfence defensive spend geographically; (ii) graduating from one-city profitability to multi-city scale requires repeating the seeding cost at each new launch, against an incumbent who already has the next city seeded. The strategy works as a sustainable local business; it is unlikely to dethrone Deliveroo nationally.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 5 marks: 1 for the network-of-networks framing (cribsheet-required), 1 for each of two distinct tactical examples (hard-side attack, niche/category attack, exclusivity deals, superior local product, etc. — at least two distinct angles), 2 for effectiveness commentary that explicitly addresses both the local viability AND the scale-out difficulty. Mirrors paper2024_q12 (Uber sub-network attack) marking conventions: students who don't frame around 'network of networks' cap at 3 marks even with good tactical examples. Specific tactical examples MUST be tied to Glasgow / a single city, not generic.

questions.question_text:
Deliveroo launches in a new city. In a typical month it spends $20,000 on local marketing (Google SEM and social ads combined) and acquires 100 new paying customers from that spend. Each acquired customer places, on average, 4 orders per month with an average order value of $50, and the typical customer is retained for 12 months before churning.

(a) Calculate the customer acquisition cost (CAC).
(b) Calculate the customer lifetime value (LTV), using the gross-revenue convention used in this course.
(c) State the LTV:CAC ratio.
(d) State whether this satisfies the typical investor minimum, and comment briefly.

Ignore other overheads. Show each step.
questions.model_answer:
**Step (a) — CAC (1 mark):** CAC = total acquisition spend / customers acquired = $20,000 / 100 = **$200 per customer**.

**Step (b) — LTV (1 mark):** LTV = revenue per order × orders per month × retention months = $50 × 4 × 12. Compute: $50 × 4 = $200 per month per customer; $200 × 12 = **$2,400 LTV per customer**.

**Step (c) — LTV:CAC ratio (1 mark):** Ratio = LTV / CAC = $2,400 / $200 = **12:1**.

**Step (d) — Investor-minimum check and comment (1 mark):** The typical investor minimum is **3:1**. A ratio of 12:1 is comfortably above this threshold, so on these single-market figures the unit economics look excellent. Honest caveat (within course concepts): this calculation uses gross order revenue, not contribution margin — Deliveroo only retains the take-rate (commission and delivery-fee share), so the *contribution-margin LTV:CAC* will be substantially lower. The figure is also for a single mature city; the calculation does not include the seeding costs (rider hourly minimum, restaurant onboarding) that are incurred before steady state is reached.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks: 1 mark per labelled step (a)-(d). Arithmetic is calculator-free by construction: $20,000 / 100 = $200; $50 × 4 = $200; $200 × 12 = $2,400; $2,400 / $200 = 12. The 3:1 investor-minimum threshold is the trigger phrase from paper2024_q2 / paper2025_q1. The contribution-margin caveat in (d) is bonus framing that demonstrates mastery — not required for the mark, which is satisfied by stating 12:1 > 3:1 and concluding the unit economics pass. Students who use net revenue / contribution margin in (b) and arrive at a different LTV should still earn (b) and (c) provided their stated convention is consistent.

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for Medium (the long-form publishing platform). For each item identified, clearly state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Approach:** Same exercise as the AirBnB / Instagram past-paper inventory questions — name the mechanism, state its type clearly, give a brief description applied to Medium. There are more mechanisms available than there are marks (1 mark per correctly identified, named, and described mechanism, capped at 6).

**(1) Content-based indirect CGM — company-generated (1 mark):** In Medium's early days, Ev Williams' team commissioned high-quality articles. These articles act as content that pulls in new readers via search engines and social shares — the canonical indirect content CGM, operating at higher than transaction frequency.

**(2) Content-based indirect CGM — user-generated (1 mark):** As the writer base grew, Medium transitioned the same CGM to user-generated content (the CG→UG transition). Articles written by users now dominate the discovery flywheel.

**(3) Two-sided network effect — writers ↔ readers (1 mark):** More writers → more articles → more reasons for readers to come; more readers → more engagement → more reason for writers to publish. Soft (not direct-social) two-sided effect.

**(4) SEO / data-scale loop (1 mark):** More published articles → more indexed pages → more long-tail search traffic → more reader acquisition without paid spend. A scale-based compounding loop layered on top of the content CGM.

**(5) Financial CGM — writer payouts / Partner Programme (1 mark):** Medium pays writers based on member engagement with their articles. This financially-incentivised mechanism attracts more writers, which feeds the two-sided network effect.

**(6) Social-capital CGM (Direct, writer side) (1 mark):** Writers share their published Medium pieces on Twitter/LinkedIn for clout and audience growth. This drives word-of-mouth-style discovery for non-Medium readers and acts as an organic referral effect for the platform.

**(Additional valid mechanisms beyond the 6 cap):** brand-scale network effect; curation / staff-picks reducing anti-network effects from variable UG quality; data network effect via personalised recommendations.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 6 marks. Award 1 mark per mechanism that is (a) named, (b) typed correctly (e.g. 'indirect content CGM — UG sub-type', 'two-sided network effect'), and (c) briefly described as applied to Medium specifically. Listing types without applying them to Medium loses marks (cf. paper2024_q13 Instagram marking note). The CG→UG split should be credited as two distinct items because they are different sub-types operating at different stages. Don't penalise students who give 5 strong items plus a weak 6th — cap at 6, take the best.

questions.question_text: Identify the dominant compounding growth mechanism present in Medium's growth model and explain how it operates. In your answer, name the CGM type explicitly and describe how the search-engine indexing of Medium articles contributes to the loop.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Name the CGM type (1 mark):** The dominant CGM on Medium is an **indirect, content-based CGM**. It is indirect because the article (the content) is what drives new-user acquisition rather than a referral link or invitation from an existing user.

**Point 2 — How it operates on Medium (1 mark):** Each published article is a discoverable artefact. Readers find articles via search engines and social shares; some of those readers go on to become repeat readers, and a fraction become writers themselves, producing more articles — feeding the loop.

**Point 3 — The SEO contribution (1 mark):** Every published article becomes a new page that Google indexes. As the article corpus grows, Medium accumulates an enormous long-tail of indexed pages targeting many different search queries — so search traffic compounds with the article count rather than scaling linearly with marketing spend.

**Point 4 — Why this is compounding rather than linear (1 mark):** Articles persist and continue to attract traffic for months or years after publication, so the CGM operates **above transaction frequency** (a reader who never publishes still keeps generating exposure for the platform every time their article shows up in someone else's search). The output of past cycles becomes the input to future cycles, which is the compounding signature.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming the indirect content CGM. 1 mark for describing the article-as-acquisition-artefact loop. 1 mark for the SEO indexing point (the question explicitly asks for it — students who skip this lose a mark). 1 mark for distinguishing compounding from linear marketing (article persistence / above-transaction-frequency). Don't double-credit students who restate the same point in two ways.

questions.question_text: Medium has a two-sided structure of writers and readers. Using concepts from the course, explain the network effect operating between the two sides and discuss why this network effect is generally considered weaker than the direct social network effect found in a product such as Snapchat.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Identify the two-sided network effect (1 mark):** Medium exhibits a **soft two-sided network effect**: more writers on the platform means more (and more varied) articles, which makes Medium more valuable to readers; more readers means more potential audience and engagement, which makes Medium more valuable to writers.

**Point 2 — How the two sides reinforce each other (1 mark):** The two sides reinforce each other indirectly — writers and readers don't necessarily know each other personally, but each side scales the value of the platform for the other. This is the same structural pattern as a content marketplace.

**Point 3 — Why it is weaker than Snapchat-style direct NE (1 mark):** In Snapchat the network effect is **direct and personal**: the value to me depends specifically on whether *my friends* are on the platform. On Medium, a reader doesn't need any specific writer to be present — they just need the platform to have *enough good articles*. The dependency is on aggregate supply, not on identity, so the per-user marginal value of an additional writer is much smaller.

**Point 4 — Consequence for growth dynamics / atomic networks (1 mark):** Because the dependency is aggregate rather than personal, Medium does not benefit from the dense **atomic network** dynamic that lets Snapchat give small friend groups full value on day one. Medium has to accumulate a large library of writers before readers experience strong network value, which is one reason its growth has been slower and less explosive than direct-social products.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for naming the two-sided NE. 1 mark for describing the bidirectional reinforcement on Medium specifically. 1 mark for the direct-vs-indirect / aggregate-vs-personal contrast with Snapchat. 1 mark for the atomic-network consequence (slower, less explosive growth). Students who only describe Medium without contrasting Snapchat cap at 2 marks — the question explicitly asks for the comparison.

questions.question_text: Medium has two distinct user populations — readers and writers — and the activation event for each side is different. Using concepts from the course, identify the activation moment for each side, explain why writer activation is harder to achieve than reader activation, and comment on which side a Medium growth team should prioritise investing in and why.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Reader activation moment (1 mark):** A reader is activated when they read an article that holds them long enough that they come back for another (the canonical 'first session that beat the random-article bar' moment). It is a low-friction, single-action activation that the recommendation system can drive.

**Point 2 — Writer activation moment (1 mark):** A writer is activated when they publish a piece that gets meaningful engagement (claps, responses, follows). The activation requires both *producing* a piece of work and *receiving* a positive social signal.

**Point 3 — Why writer activation is harder (1 mark):** Writer activation requires significantly higher effort (drafting an article is much more work than reading one), and the activation outcome is conditional on other users showing up to engage — so the activation function depends on the rest of the network being live, not just on the writer's own behaviour. This makes writer activation slower and the funnel narrower.

**Point 4 — Which side to prioritise and why (1 mark):** Prioritise **writer activation**, because writers are the harder, more valuable side — every activated writer produces ongoing content that drives reader acquisition (via the indirect content CGM and SEO loop) for months or years. Reader activation is important but more easily handled by curation and recommendation. Concentrating activation investment on the constrained side is the standard two-sided-marketplace strategy.
