questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark each: reader activation moment, writer activation moment, reasoned explanation of why writer activation is harder, prioritisation recommendation with justification. Accept either side as the priority answer if the justification is sound, but the standard course answer is writer-side because the writer is the constrained / harder / more compounding side. Students who confuse activation with retention or NaP cap at 2 marks.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Multi-part question: identify both moments, contrast their difficulty, recommend a side. All four sub-asks must be addressed.

questions.question_text: Medium serves both readers and writers, but the two sides engage with the product at very different cadences. Suggest a plausible Natural Frequency (NaP) for each side, justify the difference in cadence, and explain why a single product can sustainably hold two distinct NaPs at the same time.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Reader NaP (1 mark):** A reasonable reader NaP is around **2 articles per week (2a7)** — readers consume articles like they consume any other content feed; a couple of times per week is enough to form a habit without pressure to use the product daily.

**Point 2 — Writer NaP (1 mark):** A reasonable writer NaP is around **1 published piece per month (1p30)** — writing a long-form article is high-effort, so writer cadence is much lower; once a month is a realistic, sustainable rhythm for a typical writer.

**Point 3 — Why a single product can hold both (1 mark):** The two sides are doing different things, so their NaPs measure different actions (consumption vs production) and don't have to match. The product just needs each side to clear its own NaP often enough to keep that side retained — readers stay engaged at a consumption cadence, writers stay engaged at a production cadence, and the two-sided network effect holds them together. A product mistakenly trying to force one common NaP would likely either burn out writers (too frequent) or under-engage readers (too infrequent).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for a sensible reader NaP (any plausible reader cadence between several-per-week and weekly is fine). 1 mark for a sensible writer NaP (monthly or every-few-weeks). 1 mark for the explanation that the two NaPs measure different actions and that the product holds both because each side is independently retained at its own cadence. Reject answers that give the same NaP for both sides — that misses the entire point of the question.

questions.question_text:
Medium's content-based indirect CGM has historically operated at a higher frequency than the platform's underlying transaction frequency, and over time the company shifted the balance of the CGM from company-generated content toward user-generated content.

(a) Explain why a content CGM might be deliberately operated at a higher frequency than the product's transaction frequency. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why Medium would later transition the CGM from company-generated content to user-generated content, and identify one significant risk this transition introduces. (3 marks)
questions.model_answer:
**Part (a) — Above-transaction-frequency operation (2 marks):**

**Point 1 (1 mark):** You cannot force a user to transact more often than they naturally would — for Medium, you can't make a reader pay for a subscription more frequently or compel them to come back daily. But you can keep reminding them that the product exists in between transactions.

**Point 2 (1 mark):** A content CGM operating above transaction frequency therefore acts as an **awareness / retention reminder** — articles surfacing in search and social feeds keep Medium top-of-mind so that when the user does want to read long-form, they come to Medium rather than a competitor.

**Part (b) — CG → UG transition and its risk (3 marks):**

**Point 3 (1 mark):** Medium initially used company-generated content because Ev Williams' team could **directly control quality and cadence**, which was essential when the writer base was too small to produce enough good content of its own.

**Point 4 (1 mark):** Medium transitioned to user-generated content for **scalability**. Staff-commissioned content is bounded by headcount and budget — there are only so many editors. A large writer base can produce orders of magnitude more articles than the company ever could in-house, which is what makes the CGM compound rather than plateau.

**Point 5 (1 mark) — Risk:** The major risk is **quality variance / trust degradation**. UG content is uneven — some articles are excellent, many are mediocre or worse. If poor-quality articles dominate a reader's first impression, the platform's brand erodes and reader retention falls (an anti-network effect). Medium mitigates this with editor-curated mechanisms such as 'staff picks' and recommendation-based surfacing, but the risk is intrinsic to the transition.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: Part (a): 1 mark for the cannot-force-more-transactions point, 1 mark for the awareness/reminder mechanism. Part (b): 1 mark for why CG first (control / early-stage / quality assurance), 1 mark for why UG later (scalability beyond staff/LLM headcount), 1 mark for naming a credible risk (quality variance, trust, moderation cost — quality variance is the canonical answer). This is the canonical Logan two-part question (cf. revision_q2 / sample_q12) but applied specifically to Medium and extended with the risk component. Common student error: answering only one part — penalise heavily if part (a) or (b) is missing.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Two-part question. This is the canonical Logan example for content CGMs — both parts must be answered, and part (b) explicitly asks for a risk as well as a rationale.

questions.question_text: Substack — a newsletter-publishing platform where readers subscribe to individual writers — has emerged as a significant competitor to Medium for high-profile long-form writers. Using concepts covered on the course, explain why Substack's model is structurally threatening to Medium's two-sided network effect, and suggest one strategic response Medium could employ to defend its position.
questions.model_answer:
**Point 1 — Substack disintermediates the platform-side network effect (1 mark):** On Medium, a writer's audience belongs to *Medium*: readers come for the platform and discover writers there. On Substack, the writer owns the **direct relationship with their subscribers** (an email list). This shifts the value of the network from platform-aggregate to writer-personal — meaning Medium's two-sided NE doesn't help retain top writers, because they no longer need the platform's reader base.

**Point 2 — Hard-side attack on the constrained side (1 mark):** This is the canonical **hard-side attack** pattern (cf. Uber-vs-startup logic in paper2024_q12): Substack offers Medium's most valuable, hardest-to-acquire side — the writers — better terms (full subscriber ownership, higher revenue share). If the hard side defects, the soft side (readers) follows, and Medium's two-sided NE collapses asymmetrically.

**Point 3 — Anti-compounding effect on Medium's content CGM (1 mark):** Every top writer who moves to Substack writes one fewer article on Medium, which reduces the indexed-pages corpus, weakens Medium's SEO loop, and shrinks the ambient awareness that the indirect content CGM produces. This is anti-compounding: each defection makes the next defection slightly more attractive.

**Point 4 — Strategic response (1 mark):** A reasonable response is for Medium to give writers more of what Substack provides without giving up the platform advantages — for example, **paid newsletters with audience portability**, stronger writer-to-subscriber direct messaging, or **better revenue share via the Partner Programme** (closing the financial gap). The point is to neutralise the financial-asymmetry and ownership advantages Substack offers while keeping Medium's discovery/SEO benefits as the differentiator. (Other defensible answers: invest in editorial curation that Substack can't replicate; double down on the two-sided NE by improving discovery for new writers.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark for identifying the disintermediation / writer-owns-audience point. 1 mark for framing this as a hard-side attack on the constrained side. 1 mark for the anti-compounding consequence on Medium's content CGM and SEO loop. 1 mark for any defensible strategic response with reasoning (the most common credit-worthy answers are: better revenue share, audience-portability features, or doubled-down editorial curation as a non-replicable differentiator). Students who name course concepts explicitly (hard-side attack, two-sided NE, content CGM) earn marks more reliably than those describing the threat in generic business terms.

questions.question_text:
Medium has 100,000 weekly active readers. Internal analytics show the reader Natural Frequency (NaP) is 2 articles per week. Of the weekly active readers, 25% exceed NaP and read on average 4 articles per week, while the remaining 75% engage at exactly NaP (2 articles per week).

Calculate the total number of article-reads generated per week across the weekly active reader base. Show your working.
questions.model_answer:
**Step 1 — Split the reader base by engagement tier:**
- Above-NaP readers: 25% × 100,000 = **25,000 readers** at 4 articles/week.
- At-NaP readers: 75% × 100,000 = **75,000 readers** at 2 articles/week.

**Step 2 — Compute reads per tier:**
- Above-NaP reads: 25,000 × 4 = **100,000 article-reads/week**.
- At-NaP reads: 75,000 × 2 = **150,000 article-reads/week**.

**Step 3 — Sum:** Total = 100,000 + 150,000 = **250,000 article-reads per week**.

**Final answer: 250,000 article-reads per week.**
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks: 1 mark for splitting the base correctly into 25,000 + 75,000; 1 mark for computing reads per tier (100,000 and 150,000); 1 mark for the correct total of 250,000. Award partial credit along the chain for arithmetic slips as long as the method is correct (cf. paper2025_q15 marking convention). Calculator-free arithmetic — numbers are deliberately clean.

questions.question_text: List each of the network effects and compounding growth mechanisms present in the growth model for Snapchat. For each item, state its type and provide a brief description of its operation.
questions.model_answer:
**Network effects:**

**(1) Direct social network effect within friend groups (1 mark):** Snapchat is more useful to me when my actual friends are on it — value flows directly between users sending and receiving snaps. Crucially this network is *dense locally but sparse globally*: a small high-school cohort being fully on Snapchat is enough for the product to be valuable to its members, regardless of overall penetration. This is the textbook **atomic-network** pattern.

**(2) Data / scale network effect on the recommendation and Discover side (1 mark):** As Snapchat grows, the recommendation algorithms behind Discover, Spotlight and ad targeting improve with more usage data, lifting engagement and ad performance.

**(3) Brand / scale effects (1 mark):** At large scale Snap negotiates better unit costs on cloud, storage and bandwidth, and brand recognition lowers acquisition friction — particularly important among teen cohorts where the brand carries social cachet.

**Compounding growth mechanisms:**

**(4) Direct organic CGM (1 mark):** To use Snapchat usefully you need your friends on it, so users actively recruit their friend group by word-of-mouth. This is the dominant CGM in the early growth story.

**(5) Direct invitation CGM (1 mark):** 'Add friends' contact-sync flows let users invite their phonebook directly inside the product — a personal-utility-flavoured invitational CGM that piggy-backs on the address book.

**(6) Streaks as a CGM-flavoured retention loop (1 mark):** Streaks are not a pure CGM but operate similarly — a streak cannot be maintained alone, so each participant pulls the other back daily. This produces a viral *pull* (re-engaging lapsed friends rather than recruiting strangers) on top of the retention benefit.

**(7) Indirect content CGM via Stories / Discover (extra, for safety):** Stories cross-posted to other platforms (and Discover / publisher partner content) generate ambient awareness for non-users, drawing them into Snapchat.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per correctly named AND briefly described mechanism applied specifically to Snapchat, max 6. Naming matters — 'streaks' described purely as 'a fun feature' will not score; the candidate must frame it as a CGM-flavoured retention loop (or equivalent). The atomic-network framing on point (1) is the unlock — students who only say 'social network effect' without the dense-local / sparse-global insight are scoring the bare minimum on that point.
questions.exam_technique_notes: 6 marks → aim for 6 distinct mechanisms (a 7th is cheap insurance). Name each with course terminology (e.g. 'direct organic CGM' not just 'word-of-mouth') and tie each to Snapchat specifically.

questions.question_text: Identify the compounding growth mechanisms (CGMs) at work in Snapchat. For each, name its type using course terminology and briefly describe its operation in the Snapchat context.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) Direct organic CGM (1 mark):** Snapchat is essentially worthless to a user whose friends are not on it, so activated users actively recruit their friend group by word-of-mouth. The personal-utility motive (I want to send snaps to my friends) drives the invitations.

**(2) Direct invitation CGM (1 mark):** The in-product 'add friends' flow with contact-sync surfaces phonebook contacts and prompts the user to invite them directly — a frictionless invitational CGM piggy-backing on the address book.

**(3) Streaks as a CGM-flavoured retention loop (1 mark):** A streak requires two participants to send daily; if one lapses, the streak breaks for both. This produces a *re-engagement* viral pull — a lapsed friend gets nudged back by their counterpart — which behaves like a CGM operating on the existing user base rather than on new acquisition.

**(4) Indirect content CGM via Stories / Discover (1 mark):** Stories shared off-platform and Discover / publisher content produce ambient awareness for non-users, who then download the app — content acting as the referral vehicle rather than a person.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 1 mark per CGM, correctly named with course terminology AND tied to Snapchat. The streaks point is the differentiator — many candidates will list streaks as 'a retention feature' without recognising the viral-pull / CGM-flavoured framing. Accept either ordering of points but the four distinct mechanisms must be present for full marks. Three of four also acceptable for 3/4.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Use the precise course terms ('direct organic CGM', 'direct invitation CGM', 'indirect content CGM'). Mark Logan flags streaks specifically as a CGM-flavoured mechanic, not just a retention gimmick — frame it that way.

questions.question_text: Using network-effects concepts studied on the course, explain why Snapchat's network was valuable to its early users despite Snapchat having only a tiny share of the global messaging market. In your answer, refer explicitly to the structure of Snapchat's network.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) Direct social network effect, but locally measured (1 mark):** Snapchat carries a direct (one-sided) social network effect — value to me increases as my friends join. The relevant 'network' for measuring that value, however, is *my friend group*, not the global user base.

**(2) Dense locally, sparse globally — the atomic-network pattern (1 mark):** Snapchat's network was dense within small friend cohorts (e.g. a single high-school year group) and sparse across the rest of the world. As long as one cohort was densely connected, the product had genuine value for its members on day one — independent of overall penetration.

**(3) Atomic networks as the unit of value (1 mark):** This is the textbook atomic-network pattern: the smallest viable network is a friend group of perhaps 5–20 teenagers, and once that atomic unit is dense, the product works. Growth then proceeds atomic-network by atomic-network (cohort to cohort), not by uniform global spread.

**(4) Why the global-share framing is misleading (1 mark):** A small global share would be fatal for a product whose network effect is measured globally (e.g. a marketplace), but is irrelevant for Snapchat because no user cares whether someone in another country uses it. Comparing Snapchat to global incumbents on share alone misses the structure of the network.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks. The dense-locally / sparse-globally framing AND the atomic-network terminology are essentially required for full marks. A candidate who simply says 'social network effect' without distinguishing local from global density is scoring at most 1–2. Credit awarded for explicitly contrasting Snapchat's structure with networks where global density matters (marketplaces, search).
questions.exam_technique_notes: Use the explicit terms 'atomic network', 'dense locally, sparse globally', and 'smallest viable network'. The question is testing whether you can articulate the structural distinction, not just name network effects in general.

questions.question_text: Snapchat's growth team observes that, of every 1,000 users acquired in a given week, roughly 400 send a snap and receive one back within their first 48 hours, while the remaining 600 do not. Six months later, the team plots a cohort retention chart for that week's signups. Using concepts studied on the course, describe what shape you would expect the chart to take, and what overall retention rate you would expect at the 6-month mark. Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) Identify the activation moment (1 mark):** Snapchat's activation is sending a snap that gets a snap back — the first reciprocal exchange. The 400 users who completed this within 48 hours are *activated*; the 600 who did not are *non-activated*. This is the standard activation-inequality split for a social-media product.

**(2) Shape — steep early drop from non-activated churn (1 mark):** The cohort chart will fall steeply over the first few weeks as the 600 non-activated users churn out almost entirely (social-media non-activated users typically churn within days). The curve will look almost vertical at the start.

**(3) Shape — levelling off as the activated cohort persists (1 mark):** After the activation phase, the curve flattens dramatically because the activated 400 are stickily engaged — friend-network lock-in plus streaks make their retention much higher than the early slope suggests.

**(4) Apply the ~60% retention floor to the activated portion (1 mark):** Mark Logan's social-media rule of thumb is that *activated* users retain at roughly 60% over the medium term. Of the 400 activated users, ~60% (≈240) should still be active at 6 months. The 600 non-activated users contribute essentially nothing. Total cohort retention at 6 months ≈ 240 / 1,000 = **~24%** — a healthy outcome by social-media standards because the floor is being held by the activated half of the cohort, not because the headline number is impressive.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks. Awarded for: (1) naming the Snapchat-specific activation moment (reciprocal snap), (2) describing the steep-then-flat shape, (3) explaining *why* it flattens (activation inequality), (4) applying the ~60% retention floor to the *activated* segment specifically — not to the whole cohort. A candidate who applies 60% to the full 1,000 (giving 600) misunderstands the floor and loses the final mark. The ~24% figure is the target answer; ±5pp accepted with sound reasoning.
questions.exam_technique_notes: The 60% floor applies to *activated* users only. Splitting the cohort by activation status before applying the floor is the move the marker is looking for.

questions.question_text: Snapchat's 'streaks' feature shows the number of consecutive days two friends have exchanged snaps, and breaks if a day is missed. Using concepts covered in the course, comment on streaks as an engagement-intensity and natural-frequency mechanism.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) Streaks formalise a daily natural frequency (1 mark):** Messaging products run at a daily cadence — a plausible Snapchat NaP framing is something like 'send a snap to 2 friends per day' (2s1). Streaks make this NaP explicit and visible, turning it into a commitment device: a 100-day streak is, in effect, a 100-day NaP commitment.

**(2) High engagement intensity for the social-media category (1 mark):** Daily reciprocal exchange with multiple friends is genuinely high engagement intensity — much higher than e.g. BeReal's once-per-day single post. Streaks lift the floor on engagement intensity rather than just nudging users back.

**(3) Risk — anti-network-effect / spam edge (1 mark):** Pushed too hard, daily-streak pressure can cross into spam: notifications and guilt-driven re-engagement risk anti-network effects (users associate the app with obligation rather than fun). A well-designed streak balances commitment with not punishing genuinely busy users — otherwise the very mechanic that drives intensity drives churn.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks. Looking for explicit use of the course terms 'natural frequency' / 'NaP', 'engagement intensity', and at least one of 'commitment device' or 'anti-network effects'. A candidate who only describes streaks ('they encourage daily use') without naming the underlying concepts scores at most 1. Credit also given for the alternative framing that streaks act as a CGM-flavoured retention loop, provided the NaP / engagement-intensity language is still present.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Mark the question as fundamentally about engagement intensity — name the NaP cadence (daily) and explain how streaks formalise it.

questions.question_text: Snapchat launched in 2011 from a single American high-school cohort and within a few years had built a globally significant social network. By contrast, Google+ launched in 2011 leveraging Google's existing 1-billion-user account base and was effectively dead within five years; Meta's Threads launched in 2023 with 41.8M DAUs by day two but retention collapsed by ~79% within weeks. Using network-effects concepts studied on the course, provide a reasonable explanation for Snapchat's success against the failures of Google+ and Threads.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) Snapchat as an atomic-network success (1 mark):** Snapchat seeded *dense* networks one cohort at a time (high-school year groups). The smallest viable network — perhaps 10–20 friends — was achievable in a single school. Once that atomic unit was dense, the product worked completely for its users regardless of global penetration.

**(2) Google+ and Threads as sparse-global launches (1 mark, essentially required):** Both Google+ and Threads launched by *replicating an existing identity graph* (Google accounts; Instagram follows). The resulting network was sparse with respect to the new product's actual use case — the people I follow on Instagram for visual content are not the people I want for Twitter-style discourse. Headline DAU numbers were inflated by onboarding friction-removal but the underlying network density for the *relevant* use case was thin.

**(3) Anti-network effects of an empty room (1 mark):** When a new user joined Google+ or Threads, the experience was an empty feed — content the user didn't care about, posted by people not posting for that context. That immediately produces anti-network effects: bad first experience, no reason to return. Snapchat avoided this because new users joined into an already-dense friend cohort.

**(4) Strategy contrast — cohort-by-cohort vs national launch (1 mark):** Snapchat's growth pattern was atomic-network-by-atomic-network: dense one cohort, then expand to the next adjacent cohort (siblings, neighbouring schools, etc.). Google+ and Threads attempted national/global launches before any single sub-network was dense — exactly the sparse-network anti-pattern Mark Logan flags.

**(5) Why headline numbers misled in 2011 / 2023 (1 mark):** Both Google+ (auto-enrolled Google account holders) and Threads (auto-imported Instagram followers) booked huge initial DAU figures from onboarding tricks. These collapsed because the underlying network was sparse for the new use case — the trick gets people through the door but cannot manufacture density. Snapchat never reported flattering top-line numbers but had something neither competitor had: a dense, working atomic network.
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 5 marks. Point (2) — the dense-vs-sparse network framing — is essentially required, mirroring the marking guidance on the canonical Threads question (paper2024_q15). The candidate must identify Snapchat as an *atomic-network* success and Google+/Threads as *sparse-global* failures. Awarded any 5 of the points above provided point (2) is present. Recognising that headline DAUs from onboarding tricks mask network density (point 5) is a strong differentiator.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Frame Snapchat as the success-case mirror of the Threads / Google+ failures. Use the explicit terms 'atomic network', 'dense locally, sparse globally', and 'sparse with respect to the relevant use case'.

questions.question_text: Snapchat has built a deeply entrenched friend-network among western teenagers, with high streak counts and strong daily engagement. Explain how a start-up could nevertheless attempt to attract participants away from Snapchat's network. State the general strategic approach and give specific examples of actions that could be taken.
questions.model_answer:
**(1) General strategic point — Snapchat is a network of networks (1 mark):** Although Snapchat's friend-network is famously sticky, it is not a single homogeneous network — it is a network of friend-cohort sub-networks (a school year, a friend group, a specific city's teen scene). The network effects across the whole are weaker than the headline scale suggests, so Snapchat is attackable by a sub-network attack on individual cohorts. To get full marks, frame the answer around this 'network of networks' insight.

**(2) Specific example — target a single cohort with a superior product fit (1 mark):** Pick one identifiable cohort (e.g. a particular university intake, a specific country's teen segment, a specific interest community) and build a product experience that is materially better for *them* — a feature set, content type or moderation regime that fits their needs better than Snapchat's generic offering. Once that atomic network flips, expand to adjacent cohorts.

**(3) Specific example — hard-side seeding via influencers (1 mark):** Pay or sign creators / influencers who are central to a target cohort to publish exclusively on the new platform. Their followers in that cohort then have a concrete reason to switch, dragging the dense friend sub-network with them.

**(4) Specific example — exploit an anti-network-effect weakness (1 mark):** Identify a category of user that Snapchat is poorly serving (e.g. heavier-content users frustrated by ephemerality, or a sub-community uneasy about Discover content / ads / safety) and build for them. Snapchat's anti-network effects in that segment become the start-up's pull. (Equivalent credit: attack on a feature axis Snapchat structurally cannot match — e.g. higher-fidelity persistent content for a creator sub-community.)
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 4 marks. The 'network of networks' framing on point (1) is required for full marks — listing tactics without that framing tops out at 2/4. Specific examples must be tied to Snapchat's actual sub-network structure (friend cohorts), not generic. Hard-side seeding (influencers) and anti-network-effect exploitation are both valid; either earns the relevant mark.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Mirror the Uber sub-network-attack answer pattern: lead with 'network of networks', then give specific Snapchat-tied examples. Don't list generic tactics.

questions.question_text:
Snapchat's growth team measures its direct invitation CGM and finds that, on average, each user in a cycle generates 0.5 new sign-ups in the next cycle (i.e. v = 0.5).

4,000 users obtained from linear marketing are used to seed the CGM, which then runs through multiple cycles until exhaustion. Assume no noise or error.

(a) How many additional users sign up during the first cycle (i.e. with how many users does cycle 2 commence)?
(b) What is the growth multiplier (GM)?
(c) How many users in total will the CGM have produced when it has run to exhaustion (including the original seed)?

Give answers to zero decimal places.
questions.model_answer:
**(a) Cycle-2 starting users (1 mark):** cycle₂ = v × cycle₁ = 0.5 × 4,000 = **2,000 users**.

**(b) Growth multiplier (1 mark):** GM = 1 / (1 − v) = 1 / (1 − 0.5) = 1 / 0.5 = **2.0**.

**(c) Total users at exhaustion (1 mark):** Total = seed × GM = 4,000 × 2.0 = **8,000 users** (which is the seed plus the geometric sum 2,000 + 1,000 + 500 + 250 + … = 4,000 across all subsequent cycles).
questions.marking_scheme_notes: 3 marks, one per part. (a) tests application of v as the cycle-to-cycle ratio; (b) tests the GM = 1/(1−v) formula; (c) tests the seed × GM result and ideally an explicit recognition that the GM already bakes in the geometric sum to exhaustion. A candidate who correctly states GM = 2.0 but then computes total as seed × v or forgets to include the seed loses the final mark. Mental arithmetic only — all values are clean.
questions.exam_technique_notes: Memorise GM = 1/(1−v) and total = seed × GM. The cycle-2 starting number is just v × seed. All three parts fall out of those two relationships.
